subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO POLICY AS TO DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL AVIATION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO POLICY AS TO DOMESTIC AND INTERNATIONAL AVIATION
speechtext:
I should like to make a statement of the policy of the government on civil air transport. First with respect to domestic aviation:
1.	During the war a remarkable expansion of Canadian aviation has taken place-in the training of air and ground personnel, in the construction of airports and air navigation facilities, in the manufacture of aircraft, and in the extension of air transport services. Details of this expansion in aviation cannot be revealed at present, and therefore its magnitude is not generally appreciated. The Canadian government is aware of the importance of the developments in aviation now in progress and intends that the people of Canada shall benefit from them to the fullest possible extent.
2.	The expansion of air transport services during the period of the war has been confined to war requirements. Canada has concentrated on the development of the British Commonwealth air training plan and on combat flying and, as a result, by agreement with our allies, military air transport in the

Civil Air Transport
northwest has largely been undertaken by the United States army and on the northeast ferry routes by the ferry commands. When war necessities permit and suitable equipment can be obtained, the government will encourage the further development within Canada of air transport services, to supplement and form part of an up-to-date transportation system for Canada by land, water r and air. Transport by air requires close 1 supervision on the part of the government.
] The board of transport commissioners will be ; responsible for regulating traffic matters and 5 for allocating new routes apart from the lines brought under the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act. The civil aviation branch of the Department of Transport will be responsible for the administration of traffic and safety regulations and for the physical development of airways. The government intends to plan a number of routes suitable for post-war air services and offering traffic possibilities that [DOT] will warrant a service. These routes will make use of aerodromes that have been developed for war purposes. The government will also continue to develop airports and other facilities for weather reporting and communications, which will contribute to the expansion of Canadian air transport.
3.	While the employment in a peace-time air transport service of all the air and ground personnel of the Royal Canadian Air Force and all the men and women now employed in the aircraft industry in Canada will be impossible, a considerable number will be absorbed into the peace-time aviation industry. To this end the government has undertaken the design of distinctive Canadian types of transport aircraft suitable for post-war industry, in the hope that, when the war ends, a part at least of the equipment for Canadian air transport will be furnished by Canadian factories.
4.	Trans-Canada Air Lines will continue to be the instrument of the government in maintaining all trans-continental air transport services and in operating services across international boundary lines and outside Canada. The government will encourage the company to obtain modern aircraft which will keep present services up to modern standards and will expand these services to the fullest extent that post-war conditions permit. The development of supplementary routes will continue to be left to private enterprise, unless considerations of public interest indicate that certain of these routes should be designated by the government as routes to be operated by T.C.A. The operations of T.C.A. will continue to be limited to important services
of a mainline character, where the volume of passenger and mail traffic would justify it.
With respect to international aviation:
5.	Canada has a geographical position that will enable it to play an important part in the development of international air transport routes. During the war, the development of international civil air routes must be deferred in favour of military aviation. Canada to-day is the fourth greatest military air power among the united nations, and in the postwar period Canada can make an equally great contribution to civilian air transport.
6.	The future of international air transport will be determined in large measure by negotiations between the governments of the united nations. The policy of the government at the moment in dealing with all questions which affect international air transport is to make temporary arrangements, leaving the issues open so that Canada may be able to support, in international negotiations when they take place, whatever policy appears best at that time. The government, however, intends to press vigorously for a place in international air transportation consistent with Canada's geographical position and progress in aviation. All concessions and privileges that have been granted by Canada to other countries as part of the war effort will terminate at the end of the war or almost immediately thereafter.
7.	T.C.A. has by its charter the right to operate international air transport services and has already been designated as the instrument of the Canadian government in air transport service across the north Atlantic, and in Canadian services to the United States. The fact that international negotiations of great importance must shortly take place confirms the wisdom of government policy under which its freedom of action in international negotiations is not limited by the existence of private interests in international air transport services.
8.	The government has established an interdepartmental committee on international civil aviation to advise it on all matters of international air transport which affect Canada, and particularly on the attitude which Canada should adopt towards post-war developments. This committee has already been at work for a considerable time.
9.	The problems of international air transport are, of course, immense and cannot be solved by one country. We are determined, however, that our influence on the course
Civil Air Transport

of events will be in the direction of international co-operation and collaboration. The Canadian government is in complete agreement with the United Kingdom government that "some form of international collaboration will be essential if the air is to be developed in the interests of mankind as a whole, trade served, international understanding fostered and international security-gained."
Conclusion:
10.	The policy of the Canadian government on air transport may be summed up as follows:
(a)	The government sees no good reason for changing its policy that Trans-Canada Air Lines is the sole Canadian agency which may operate international air services.
(b)	Within Canada, Trans-Canada Air Lines will continue to operate all transcontinental systems, and such other services of a mainline character as may from time to time be designated by the government. Competition between air services over the same route will not be permitted whether between a publicly-owned service and a privately-owned service or between two privately-owned services. There will remain a large field for the development of air transport in which private Canadian companies may participate, and, while preventing duplication of services, the government will continue to encourage private companies to develop services as traffic possibilities may indicate.
(c)	In order to prepare for forthcoming international negotiations on air transport, the government is studying carefully the problems which will have to be dealt with in the negotiations.
(d)	The Canadian government strongly favours a policy of international collaboration and co-operation in air transport and is prepared to support in international negotiations whatever international air transport policy can be demonstrated as being best calculated to serve not only the immediate national interests of Canada but also our overriding interest in the establishment of an international order which will prevent the outbreak of another world war.

maintopic: CONFERENCE TO CONSIDER POST-WAR PROBLEMS- CANADIAN PARTICIPATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, March 31, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Caldwell) asked, as reported at page 1725 of Hansard, whether Canada would participate in the conference to be held in the United States on April 27 to consider long range post-war food problems; and if so, how and by whom this country would be represented.
May I say in reply that the Canadian government warmly welcomes the initiative of the President of the United States in issuing invitations for the discussion of questions connected with the distribution and consumption of food in the post-war world, and will be represented at these discussions. How and by whom will be stated in due course.

subtopic: EMPLOYEES IN ONTARIO BRANCH-REFERENCE TO QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE RAISED ON MARCH 31
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday's orders of the day the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) raised a question of privilege concerning the reply made by the Department of Munitions and Supply to a question of the hon. member regarding Lawrence B. Lougheed. It was the contention of the hon. member that incorrect information had been given in the reply, inasmuch as the reply stated that Lawrence B. Lougheed was not an employee of the oil control branch, whereas evidence taken under oath in a court case in Toronto would indicate that he was.
I now find that the reply given to the question is quite correct. Lawrence B. Lougheed is not now, nor has he ever been, an employee of the oil control branch. I am informed that Lawrence B. Lougheed is an enforcement officer of the wartime prices and trade board. Had the question been framed in more general terms this information would have been given. As it was, the question asked specifically whether Mr. Lougheed was an employee of the oil control branch; and a specific answer was given.

subtopic: MONTREAL TRAMWAYS STRIKE-TELEGRAM FROM PRESIDENT OF LOCAL 790

speechtext:
On the orders of the day:
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker, a short time ago I received a telegram from Mr. Elphege Beaudoin, president of local 790, and president of the provincial federation of labour, with regard to the Montreal tramways strike. It reads as follows:
Jean-Frangois Pouliot, M.P.,
Ottawa.
As a result of an illegal strike my own members are unable to go back to work. Those who want to work are forced to pay one dollar to the Canadian brotherhood. Three of my men were beaten this morning. We are loyal citizens who have always respected the laws of the country and we have a right to expect protection from government authorities. It is enough that we were robbed of our authority as a party to illegal contract without having to pay a penalty in order to be able to return to work. In the name of justice I demand immediate action from the government. If we are unable to get justice in this case blood might be shed in the streets between the workers members of the A.F. of L. and the Canadian brotherhood who perpetrated this illegal strike.
Elphege Beaudoin,
President,
Local 790, President of the Provincial Federation of Labour.
If it would be of any help I am ready to go to Montreal at my own expense to look into this matter and to report to the minister in due course.

I do not know that I can say anything more, except that the first responsibility for the maintenance of law and order rests upon the civil government of the city of Montreal. I think that is clearly understood by everyone in this house.
On the orders of the day

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hon. members have just heard His Honour the Speaker read a communication from His Excellency the Governor General to the effect that it is expected that the Deputy of His Excellency will proceed to another place this afternoon or this evening to give assent to certain bills. The house will recall that on March 26 two bills were passed, one for granting to His Majesty aid for national defence and security and the other to grant certain sums of money for the public service for the financial year ending March 31, 1944. The government hopes that at the same time it will be possible to have the royal assent given to the supplementary estimates which during the last day or two have been under consideration in committee of the whole.
At the moment we have planned to have the deputy of the governor general present at a quarter to six o'clock this afternoon. If the estimates have not been passed by that time it will be necessary for the government to ask hon. members to sit this evening to see if we cannot have the royal assent given to the supplementary estimates before eleven o'clock to-night. Hon. members will recall that I said the government hoped we might be able to have the Easter adjournment begin on April 16, which is a fortnight from to-day. I am afraid that jf this measure and one or two others which we are concerned about are not completed by that time it may be necessary to shorten the Easter recess more than we had hoped it would be shortened.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
I am somewhat confused as to the necessity for the rush in putting through the further supplementary estimates. I do not direct my question to the Prime Minister; I direct it to the Minister of Finance. The other evening the Minister of Finance asked us to vote certain items in the further supplementary estimates on the basis that if they were not passed that evening the civil service might conceivably have to go without their pay at the end of the month. I ask this question only for purposes of clarification, but it is very necessary that the minister answer it. We are now being asked to finish up the further supplementary estimates in order that they, as well as the items which were passed in such a rush and on that basis, may be given royal assent this evening. If that is so, then the obligation is upon the Minister of Finance to indicate what was the necessity for the speed
Business oj the House

which was indicated iwhen he asked us to expedite the matter on that particular occasion. The procedure was irregular and it placed us in a very embarrassing position; we were faced with either meeting the government's wishes or seeming to hold up, as we thought and as we were told by the government, the pay of the civil service. I should like the minister to clarify that. There may be an answer, but it does seem to me that time after time we are being asked to press and push things through. This opposition is here for the purpose of examining carefully the expenditures of the government, and there are tremendous expenditures. We are not objecting to them, but we do want to have the opportunity of examining, so far as we may with the limited means at our disposal, each item of government expenditure. Some of these items run up to almost three-quarters of a million dollars. The minister ought to explain to the house why he asked that these estimates be pushed through so hurriedly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I explained that in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) on the day of the evening in question.
I am sorry I was not in the house on that occasion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman will find what I said in Hansard, but I will repeat it for his information and for the information of hon. members.
So far as I know the government never issues cheques unless there is some authority for the expenditure, unless the House of Commons has passed upon it. But there have been occasions in the past when after items were approved by the House of Commons-
After resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, a resolution or an item. Where it has been passed upon by the house the Minister of Finance has taken it upon himself to direct the comptroller of the treasuiy to issue cheques, knowing that the legislation confirming wdiat had been done would be passed later. That was why I wanted these estimates through that night- because the civil servants had either to be paid the next day or told to wait. I therefore picked out the most pressing items and asked the house to pass them, which it was good enough to do on the understanding that hon. members would have the fullest opportunity of discussing anything in connection

with these items on a particular item I named. That discussion is going on at the present time.
With regard to royal assent, beginning yesterday morning telephone calls have been coming in from various departments wanting money. I do not want to press too far this practice of paying out money without legal authority, and I do not propose to do so if I can help it. We have passed two interim supply bills, one of them on March 26 providing for payments in the present fiscal year. Those payments are being clamoured for at the present time, and yesterday and to-day we have had to tell them that they cannot get their money until to-morrow. That is on the assumption that there will be royal assent to-day to the bills which have already gone through.
They are not held up, in any event.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. With regard to the supplementary estimates I do not know exactly what the position is, but the official who is sitting with me here told me, when they were discussed the other evening, that very early in April, there would be a pressing demand for money to be paid under these supplementary estimates. I assume that that is the case, but I do not know just what items are affected. My information on that is not definite.
I would point out that I brought these supplementary items before the house one week ago to-day, confidently expecting that both the supplementary estimates and the interim supply bill would go through that afternoon. Year after year the supplementary estimates, which are merely for the purpose of carrying out existing commitments the principle of which has been passed upon at the previous session, which introduce nothing new, and which presumably have been fully debated, go through in half an hour or an hour. But instead of that we have been a week on these supplementary estimates, and I have had to keep pushing back my budget resolutions from day to day. Hon. gentlemen know the pressing nature of those resolutions. I am running myself into grave difficulties by deferring the placing of those resolutions before the house. There is also the mutual aid bill which it is most embarrassing at the present time for us not to have passed. I do not think I am asking the house for anything unreasonable when I place these supplementary estimates before them on one Friday and we go through to another Friday without having taken anything else up in the meantime, not a thing so far as I can remember-there was the debate on the

Business oj the House
motion to go into supply on Monday and Tuesday, but I could not help that debate-I do not think I am asking anything unreasonable when I request the house this afternoon and if necessary this evening to help me put through these supplementaries. They bring not a single new thing before the house. There is nothing in them except to carry out existing commitments. Members during this session, as soon as we get to the main estimates, and I am willing to get to them as soon as possible, will have an opportunity of debating upon them anything they might wish to raise on these items. But we cannot do all our debating in the early days of the session. You cannot press everything into those early days. Important legislation is waiting to come down. There are the budget resolutions, the arrangement with regard to last year's taxes, and the war appropriation, which we have not touched at all, which we cannot get to at all. There is also the mutual aid bill, which is most urgent. In view of all this I think it is only reasonable to ask the house to help expedite the passing of these supplementaries.

There is a very good reason why at this session there has been perhaps a little more extended debate than usual on the further supplementary estimates. I remember distinctly what happened in the dying days of the last session. The labour department, for example, brought on its estimates only two or three days before the session closed. It is all very well to say that hon. members could have had all the time they liked to debate those estimates. True, but every one realizes the atmosphere of the house in the dying days of a session and the invisible pressure which every member feels in speeding up business. I am not seeking to place the responsibility for that upon any one, but I am just pointing out that there is that feeling when the house is trying to draw its business to a close. One of the reasons why the further supplementary estimates have engaged the attention of the house to a greater extent on this occasion is that at the end of last session members had not entirely exhausted their questions and their desire for information on these items.

I was just going to say precisely what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) has said. If we were assured that at this session the estimates would be taken up in such a manner that we can discuss the various matters that come under them I have no doubt that the passage of these supplementary estimates would be greatly facilitated. Hon. members will recall that when we adjourned last session on August 1 the labour estimates came on only a
few hours before we adjourned and I remember distinctly that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mclnnis) protested vigorously against the delay in bringing down those estimates. The fact that we were not able to discuss them at that time as fully as we should have liked accounts I think for the more extended discussion now. So far as we are concerned, although I have not had an opportunity of consulting with my colleagues since this matter arose, I think I can say we are prepared to assist the minister in putting these estimates through, on the understanding that we shall not do as we have done in other sessions, leave the passing of the main estimates until the end of the session, when they cannot be given adequate consideration.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) mentioned the Easter recess. I think the duty of the house is to give thorough consideration to the business coming before it and we should not rush the business in order to get away for Easter. The reason some of us were anxious that the house should adjourn for a fairly long period at Easter was that we have been asked to assist various organizations in the promotion of the victory loan. Some of us planned to go back home to say a word in regard to the campaign. We are anxious to do that. But we should give thorough consideration to the matters before us in the house. I realize that the minister is anxious to get the budget resolutions through, and, although I do not know what is in the minister's mind regarding the mutual aid bill, I know enough from the newspapers and from statistics I have seen to realize that that may be a pressing matter. If we know that when the estimates come up we shall have ample opportunity to discuss the matters we wish to discuss, there is no reason why this comparatively small estimate-it is only $2,694,000 out of over $560,000,000-should not be passed. The trouble is that we have been discussing here what we should have discussed on the main estimates.

May I
say just a word? I am not going to occupy much time, because we have already taken up time which could have been spent on the estimates. Our parliamentary experience here dates back to 1936; and I do not believe, with all the talk that has gone on in this chamber respecting estimates, we have ever seen one item reduced by one dollar. This is significant. It means that except for the principle involved we might just as well accommodate the minister and say that we will pass the estimates and talk about them afterwards.

Oh, no.
Business oj the House

I knew you would say
"oh, no"; that is why I modified the statement by saying "except for the principle involved". I have often wondered why the whips of each party could not get together on the matter of estimates and let us present to the ministers concerned the estimates we are particularly interested in, so that when their department is called they might be the first to be discussed. In this way we would facilitate the business of the session by not leaving important estimates to be discussed at the end of the session. So far as this group is concerned we would like to accommodate the minister and get these estimates through this afternoon.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: May I say one word regarding what has been said, as to having the estimates down a little earlier.
It is as to having them discussed at an earlier stage. They are down early enough.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I beg my hon. friend's pardon-having them discussed and voted on at an early date. A week ago to-day I was unavoidably absent from the house, but I requested one of my colleagues to ask hon. members if they would allow us to call two departments simply that estimates might be proceeded with on a Thursday or Friday, when there is no risk of losing an opportunity of early discussion through some amendment on the motion to go into supply being presented. That very simple proposal has not yet been acceded to. If it were, it would enable the government to take up on any Thursday or Friday whatever particular departmental estimates the house might have agreed to take up on either of those days. I said to the hon. members some time ago that to facilitate the passing of the estimates with as little loss of time as possible, the government was prepared to consider referring certain of the estimates to standing committees, and with this in view one of the departments which it was suggested might be called was the Department of Fisheries. It had been my intention, had an item in that department been called, to move very shortly thereafter that the estimates of that department be referred to the standing committee on fisheries, as a test of how that particular method of procedure might work out-all with a view to getting ahead with consideration of estimates. I imagine hon. members have not realized that such was the motive of the government. We have been anxious to get the estimates before the house. But these other measures which have been considered are of an exceptional character, and we have had to proceed with them first.

As to the Easter recess, one of the reasons the government was anxious to have a fortnight's recess is the one which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned. It was hoped that hon. members would, as we felt sure they would, take advantage of their presence in their constituencies to speak on behalf of the victory loan. But there is another reason. It is not a desire on the part of the government to obtain a holiday, or to have anyone have what might by some be regarded as a prolonged recess. From the government's point of view it is to give some of us an opportunity of having that careful discussion of matters of policy, over a period of days, which we cannot get when the house is sitting from day to day, but which is very necessary as a part of the work of government in this time of war.

I think the Prime Minister discussed with the leaders of the groups the possibility of referring certain departments to committees-which we in this group approved. Did that meet with the approval of the various parties in the house? If so why could we not do it?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I heard from my hon. friend that he approved, and I believed his group would. I had every reason to believe that others would be prepared to accept one department or two departments as I have indicated, and it was for that reason I had asked particularly for the Department of Fisheries. Had any exception been taken at the time of proposing the motion, it would of course have been withdrawn.

Arising out of the statement made by the Prime Minister in connection with referring the estimates to a committee, I did not apprehend until after reflection that perhaps he was indicating that our group had in some way given consent to the reference of any of the estimates to a committee. That is a matter upon which we want to reserve judgment at the moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I did say I had had approval of the idea from the hon. member from Rosetown-Biggar, and that I had proposed to bring the matter up formally, but if that exception should be taken when I introduced the motion I would not press it. I meant by that that any further word as to the attitude of others would, I imagine, be intimated to the house in the course of the discussion.

PRIVILEGE-MR. CLOUTIER CELANESE FACTORY AT DRUMMONDVILLE-REPORTED SHORTAGE OF SUPPLIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I rise to a question of privilege? I have received a telegram from a citizen of my home town of Drummondville which reads as follows:
Approximately 600 employees Celanese will be dismissed in a few days unles immediate intervention hon. Minister of Munitions and Supply. Here is summary of facts. Celanese requires five carloads per month anhydric acetic acid. Controller chemical products just rationed Celanese two cars per month which will reduce production and labour twenty per cent. Information proves that Canada produces [DOT] enough of this acid for requirements of this country but exports large quantities to England not for military purposes but for production artificial silk which is afterwards exported to Canada. Should make inquiry in house immediately to assert Drummondville interests.
I would like to ask what measures the Minister of Munitions and Supply will take to avoid this situation in my locality.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CLOUTIER CELANESE FACTORY AT DRUMMONDVILLE-REPORTED SHORTAGE OF SUPPLIES
speechtext: The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of this question. I consulted with the chemicals controller, and am advised by him that the firm in question, which is the Celanese company, knew six months ago that a period of from six weeks to two months would be required to change over the plant making this particular chemical. The suggestion is that we cut off our exports to England so that this plant be not interrupted, but I may say that we have a contract with the United Kingdom Ministry of Supply to furnish certain quantities of this product monthly, and we know that the ministry rely on it for certain war production. We intend to maintain our shipments, and we shall do all we can to keep the shortage of supply to the Celanese company to a vminimum. I might add that the Celanese company is the only user in Canada of this product, and we believe that they could, with- six months' notice, have built up a stockpile to meet a situation which they knew to be inevitable.

speechtext:

Under the order
in council in volume 6 page 177, of proclamations and orders in council, relating to the war, wide powers are given to inspectors in connection with the enforcement of the cost-of-living bonus. As this is the only opportunity that will arise to discuss this order in council I wish to do so at this time, and with particular reference to the statement made to-day by the Minister of Munitions and Supply regarding enforcement officers.
It should be the aim of the government to enforce war-time regulations fairly and squarely and without regard to persons. I am not here to argue that legislation such as this should not be strictly enforced. Anyone who will commit offences against
Supply-Finance

war-time legislation, whether it is in the form of a statute or an order in council, is entitled to no consideration. I am not going to deal to-day with the question of the impropriety of having legislation as important as this in the form of an order in council, but I do object to the powers that are given to inspectors and enforcement officers under this and other like orders in council.
Under the order in council setting up the cost-of-living bonus the inspectors have powers that are not possessed under the common law or under many statutes. They have the power to examine orally, either alone or in the presence of another person, as they see fit, every person whom they find on the premises or in a place where they have reasonable cause to believe the person to be or to have been employed. Here the government sets up by order in council a group of persons called inspectors, who have the right to try a man before he comes to court. In ordinary proceedings there is not that right. And these inspectors have the right to insist upon receiving an answer to every question that they pose. That is bad enough, but when in other branches of government you find that the government is appointing enforcement officers who go through this country and induce the commission of offences during their investigation, I think the time has come to bring this to the attention of parliament.
Let me give an example. The other day I asked a question as to whether or not certain individuals were employed in the department of the oil controller, and the answer given was that they were not. Those individuals were called by the special counsel for the crown, Mr. McRuer, K.C., and they gave exidence there under examination that they were hired by the oil controller-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. Will the hon. gentleman indicate the item on which he is speaking?

I am dealing with the granting of powers under orders in council such as are granted undeT the cost-of-living bonus order in council, and illustrating my point by reference to what is going on in another department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I submit that the connection which the hon. gentleman is seeking to make between the subject matter of his discussion and the item before the committee is merely artificial. I am afraid that if hon. members are free to adopt that expedient there is nothing at all that could not be discussed

under any item, and we shall be ranging over the whole field. The item that the hon. gentleman is speaking on is item 417:
To provide, subject to allocation by the treasury board, for cost of living bonus-further amount required, $745,000.
That is the costiof-living bonus for civil servants. The hon. gentleman moves from cost-of-living bonus to civil servants, for which there are no inspectors, to cost-of-living bonus for industry, for which there are inspectors. He is discussing the inspectors in industry, but he then makes another jump to other inspectors who are doing another kind of inspection work in connection with cost-of-living bonus, and proceeds to make his speech. I contend that the connection is so remote and artificial that the hon. gentleman is out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The understanding at the time was, I took it, that some latitude would be given on almost any subject pertaining to the items that were passed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It may be true that the argument being made by the present speaker is going rather far afield, but it would be very difficult for the chairman to make a distinction. I would ask hon. members to keep as close as possible to the items before the committee.

The minister mentioned that this debate has been going on for a week. So far I have occupied about ten minutes. I protest against the attitude of the government in having enforcement officers in any department, whether under the cost-of-living bonus order in council, under the oil controller, or other departments, who are going out into the country and inducing the commission of offences when engaged in the investigation of offences. In the case of the Joy Oil company in the city of Toronto, in which one of the enforcement officers gave evidence to the effect that he was acting under instructions and his evidence was that he aided and abetted in the commission of the offence. The bonus order in council comes under the wartime prices and trade board. To-day the government has an army of inspectors, investigators and agents provocateurs, as the hon. member for York-Sunbury suggests, going up and down the country, which I suggest is totally unjustified. Look at what is done with regard to the oil regulations, in connection with which an answer was given yesterday. According to

Supply-Finance
that answer there are some twenty enforcement officers who have been, engaged directly to look after the enforcement of the regulations of the oil controller. Then the answer goes on:
A part of the duties ordinarily performed by 174 other investigators and other enforcement officers of the wartime prices and trade board include assistance from time to time in the enforcement of regulations of the oil controller.
All over this dominion we have engaged in investigations numbers of inspectors out of all proportion to the work they are doing. Let me give an example. The number of prosecutions under the wartime prices and trade board! is set out at page 1614 of Hansard. There is in each province a solicitor in charge of prosecutions. Most of those who are prosecuted plead guilty. Uip to February 28, 1943, the total amount of fines imposed in these cases was 8137,830, while the total legal fees in connection with the prosecutions was 850,415. These' prosecutors are not needed in most cases; the local crown counsel could be used. The minister often says, "Give me an example of waste." I say that right in his department to-day, in connection with investigations and prosecutions under the wartime prices and trade board, sums of money are being expended that are totally unnecessary. In the western provinces the agents of the attorney general would prosecute. Yet in every case counsel is appointed for the purpose of appearing for the prosecution, though in most cases the plea is one of guilty.
In connection with the inspectors who are appointed under the wage bonus regulations as well as the other branches administered by the Minister of Finance, I ask that he do away with this multitude of officials and prosecutors, who are doing more to arouse antagonism in the people than anything else being done by this government to-day. There is nothing that would be more likely to bring the enforcement of law into contempt than to have officers appointed by departments of the government instructed, as the men to whom I have referred swore they were instructed, to induce the commission of offences when engaged in the investigation of offences. The reply given yesterday by the minister to a question I asked was that these men are not authorized to endeavour, to induce the commission of offences in their investigation of infractions of the regulations, and I would ask the minister to have removed from office any officials who, while engaged as enforcement
officers, are found to have induced the commission of offences. If that is not done the wartime prices and trade board and the legislation it is endeavouring to enforce will be brought into disrepute just as liquor legislation was brought into disrepute some years ago. I ask, too, that the costs of administration in connection with the investigation of these offences be reduced to the minimum, and that the unnecessary and undemocratic powers granted to these officials in the course of their work be withdrawn. I would ask for the assurance of the minister that these unnecessary and what I call unjustifiable invasions of private rights be not countenanced by the department which he administers.

Last evening in discussing the cost-of-living bonus as it applied to the mounted police special guards, the minister expressed some doubt as to the wage of $1.60 a day for single men employed in that capacity. On that occasion I stated that there was no further allowance paid to these men. In checking the matter over, I find that until recently there was an allowance of $1 a day, and that now another twenty-five cents has been added. I just want to keep the record straight on that point, and to state that single men employed in that capacity do receive an extra allowance of SI .25 a day. I think it only fair to correct the record in that regard, but I would reiterate the other things I said with respect to the cost-of-living bonus.

When the house rose last night the question of old age pensions was being discussed, and that discussion would rather indicate a difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, because on March 5 the Prime Minister certainly took credit to the federal government for the old age pensions legislation, while last evening the Minister of Finance said this was the responsibility of the provinces.
I should like to ask a question concerning my own province of Manitoba, where in the past year legislation has been passed granting an additional $1.25 a month to the old age pensioners of that province, in the hope that the federal government would grant an additional $3.75, on the understanding that the federal government pays seventy-five per cent of the cost of old age pensions while the province pays twenty-five per cent. It was pointed out in this house that Alberta and British Columbia pay the extra $5 themselves. What would have to be done by the province of Manitoba to obtain this extra $3.75? If a majority of the provinces ask the government
Supply-Finance

for this additional $5 a month, to which I think the old people are entitled at least by way of a cost-of-living bonus, would that request be given favourable consideration? It is very unfair to expect these old people to provide themselves with food, shelter and [DOT] clothing on a mere $20 a month, under present conditions. It is just impossible.
The other question to which I wish to refer is in connection with labour. I have had tiffs before with the Minister of Finance about the price ceiling set-up as it applied to agriculture, and again to-day I would point out the impossible situation many farmers will encounter this summer-in fact within the next few days. I might have brought down some of my personal correspondence which shows the wages being asked' on farms. I should like to refer to the settlement this government made last year with the steel strikers, in which a basic rate of fifty-five cents an hour was set, for ordinary labour.
I believe anyone will realize that during seeding and harvesting operations on the farms a person must work at least twelve hours a day, and at the rate of fifty-five cents this amounts to $6.60. In other parts of the season of course the farm day is about ten hours.
Does that rate include bed and board?

No. I have said that the government made a settlement with the steel strikers for a rate of fifty-five cents an hour. That does not include bed and board. This is not the customary wage on the farm, but usually bed and board are included in the farm wage. But I am saying that if the people who are offering their services for work on the farm ask the same rate of pay as was granted labourers in steel production, then under this price ceiling set-up there is no minister who will rise in his place and say that agriculture, if it is forced to pay that rate, can continue to produce the necessary foodstuffs for the war. I believe these people who are to work on the farms are entitled to the same rate of pay as are the workers in the steel mills. To-day they are asking that, and rightly so. They point out that they can get fifty-five cents an hour from their work in mines and in industry, and that they are guaranteed that much by the government. That is further proof of the utterly hopeless situation with which we are faced.
I know of farmers in my district who operate highly mechanized farms. The men who can operate that machinery will not want to operate it this spring to put in the 
crop, because they can receive the rates I have mentioned from industry, and from other lines of work.
The Minister of Finance, in conjunction with the Minister of Labour must adjust this matter in the very near future. If they are to bonus organized labour, then they must bonus efficient agricultural labour to the same extent; otherwise the whole scheme of food production will collapse in the coming twelve months. That is something which must be faced, and I am asking for a statement from the minister in respect of these two matters.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
What was the second
matter?

I asked what would happen if a majority of the provinces asked for increased payment from the federal government, and what Manitoba's position would be with respect to old age pensions. My second question was with respect to farm labour.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am not in a position to enter into any discussion involving labour policy, nor would I discuss the bonusing of farm labour. If the hon. member is asking whether the government will bonus farm labour I will say simply that I do not know. It is not in my department, and I do not think I should be asked or expected to deal with it.
It arises as a result of the price ceiling policy, which comes under the minister's department.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, it does not result from the price ceiling. I do not agree with that for one moment.
The other question is one which might properly be asked me-if indeed a discussion of old age pensions is now in order. Perhaps it would be, under one or another of these items. I made very clear indeed the old age pension policy of the government when I spoke last night. Had the hon. member been in the house he would have found an answer to his question in what I said.
I read Hansard carefully to-day, and I did not find an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With regard to what would happen if a majority of the provinces wanted the limit raised, I would refer my hon. friend to my statement in the house on November 14, 1941, when I said that if all, or substantially all the provinces asked to have the limit raised the government would give consideration to their request. I made it clear last night that

Supply-Finance
I was not saying that such consideration would be favourable. I am simply saying that consideration would be given.
That situation has not arisen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; that situation has not arisen. Then, with respect to Manitoba I would say that it, in conjunction with some other provinces, has sought an amendment to the old age pensions regulations permitting it to pay supplementary allowances to old age pensioners. I understand the supplementary allowance Manitoba proposes to pay is $1.25.
The minister said last night that changes in old age pensions increases would be one of the things which would cause inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think that is quite correct.

That does not follow, because if the total amount of $31,000,000 paid out by the federal government were increased by twenty-five per cent that increase would amount to only $7,700,000-and possibly not quite that much.
On the other hand, these people are certainly entitled to some consideration. Everything else has gone up in price. How in the world can they live on less than a dollar a day? As some hon. members said last night, this is one of the things which is bad for the morale of our people and our troops.
The minister said last night that this was a matter for the provincial governments. How does he justify that statement, in view of what was said by the Premier of Ontario, as reported in to-day's Globe and Mailt This is the report:
Mothers' allowances are provincial and old age pensions a federal responsibility, he told the house. "A survey is being made and allowances will be increased *where investigation indicates need for increased allowance on the basis of an approved budget-"
And so on.
Then the report continues:
The government, the Premier said, proposes to examine all the 59,000 eases on its files and increase grants according to the need. Meanwhile, the dominion was considering lower age limits and increasing maximum pensions from $20 to $30 monthly.
Those are the words of the Premier of Ontario, and I hope what he has said is true. But bis statement does not seem to be the same as that made by the Minister of Finance last night, in which he pointed out that this was a purely provincial matter.
Has the dominion government supervision over the regulations made by the administrative branches in the various provinces? It has
come to my notice that regulations contrary to the federal act respecting old age pensions are being made, and that these regulations are in many instances to the disadvantage of the pensioners. In my view the federal government should have supervision, to see to it that there is no possibility of injustice. Many people are receiving cost-of-living bonus, while others are having increases made in their salaries. Large numbers are being given assistance of one kind or another. But in this instance we find these poor, old pepole who are unable to do anything for themselves, but who must continue to live on the pittance they are given. It is a crime to permit such a condition in this country. In view of the small amount that is involved, surely the government can do something about this matter. The premier of Ontario has indicated that he is willing to do something.
I assume the Minister of Finance has made his position clear on old age pensions and does not want to say anything further.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No; I think I have covered it.

Has the minister or his department made any representations to the provinces for larger payments, particularly to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island? The discussion here has been upon the basis of payment of $20 a month to old age pensioners. The average payment in Nova Scotia has been around $14; in Prince Edward Island it is much less. In New Brunswick I believe it is also less than in Nova Scotia. Requests for higher payments have been coming from the different provinces, and I should like to know if his department has made any direct representations to the provinces to pay the full monthly pension of $20. I have great sympathy for the old age pensioners and the difficulties they are now experiencing. Representations were made to me by some of the old age pensioners in Nova Scotia who have sons overseas that their pensions had been reduced because they were receiving assigned pay and allowances. When I first heard this complaint I would not believe it because it appeared so unreasonable, but I found that it was so. The Minister of Finance told us last night that the first responsibility of the federal government is the carrying on and the financing of the war rather than the payment of pensions. There is a tremendous deficit in his department. We were in the same position in Nova Scotia when we were first endeavouring to put old age pensions into effect; we had a deficit and we had to delay paying old age pensions. I think that
Supply-Finance

Nova Scotia and the other provinces should immediately increase the old age pension to the full amount of $20 under the present act. I contend that old age pensions should be further increased to $25 or $30 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No such representations have been made by the dominion government to the government of any province. The matter is regarded as being within the administrative jurisdiction of the provinces, and the dominion government has not made representations with regard to lowering or raising the scale. My impression of the speech from the throne delivered to the provincial legislature of Nova Scotia is that they intend to make a supplemental allowance of $5 a month.

If supplemental allowance is made payable will it be necessary to amend the old age pensions legislation? AVill that be necessary in order to pay more than $20 a month? I have heard the statement that it is not for the provinces to pay more than $20 a month, because it is prohibited by the old age pensions legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not been following this matter very carefully. On November 14, 1941, I stated to the House of Commons that if any province desired the regulations amended so that any supplemental allowance would not be regarded as income and thereby reduce the amount which the dominion could legally contribute, they would be so amended. The Department of Justice advised that the regulations could be amended in respect of one province at a time, and they have been amended with respect to several provinces, including I think Nova Scotia. If it has not been done in connection with that province, it is being done.

The position with regard to old age pensions seems to be that the minister takes the view that no further contribution should1 be made by the dominion authorities. He contends that since the coffers of the provinces are so overflowing, they ought to assume this responsibility in this time of war.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is correct.

With the government deficit being so great, speaking for myself I am bound to say that there is a good deal of common sense in that attitude. I know in New Brunswick government financing has never been so easy since confederation. This is due in large measure to the generosity of this government in dealing with the province when it vacated certain fields of taxation. The province was treated most generously. Instead of this surplus being used for a purpose such

as this, it is being diverted to other fields of endeavour, and the old people are not getting one cent of benefit.
I think the minister has a good deal of justification for his stand1, but that is not helping the situation of the old age pensioners. While the governments continue to fail to act, the old age pensioners are feeling the squeeze of the economic situation. Perhaps the discussion which has taken place here will have some effect upon the provincial governments, but I do not know. I think they will all have to assume their responsibilities. If this were peace time, I would urge the minister to act, but perhaps if we were not burdened with war this situation would not arise. I will not say anything more about old age pensions.
I should like to ask the Minister of Labour a question arising out of order in council, P.C. 1774, passed on March 9, 1942, which authorized the appointment of these inspectors in connection with the administration of the cost-of-living bonus order. I would ask him as a good Britisher if he can in his heart and conscience justify the administration of justice on the basis of section 2, paragraph (b), of this order in council? In order to clarify the position, I will read part of the order. This section reads:
2. Any person authorized by the Minister of Labour to act as an inspector shall have power to do all or any of the following things, namely:
(a)	to enter at all reasonable times any premises or place-
I do not object to that; that is the right of entry given to these inspectors.
(b)	to make such examination and inquiry as may be necessary for ascertaining whether the provisions of the wartime wages and cost-of-living bonus order-
Two other orders in council are mentioned.
-are complied with in any such premises or place.
That is giving the right to an inspector to go in and hold a preliminary inquiry, or an enquete as they call it in Quebec. It is not a judicial inquiry, simply an inquiry by a prosecuting official. You are approaching the third degree, but you have not reached it, However, in the next paragraph you reach the position of having the third degree. Listen to this:
(c)	to examine orally, either alone or in the presence of any other person as he thinks fit-
Cross-examination; that is what that means. -with respect to any matters under the wartime wages and cost-of-living bonus order-
Other orders in council are mentioned.
-every person whom he finds in such premises or place or whom he has reasonable cause to believe to be or to have been employed pursuant to the provisions of the wartime wages and eost-of-living bonus order-

He has the right to put them through the third degree.

I might have to go through a grilling at the hands of an inspector without the benefit of counsel's protection and without the benefit of reserving my rights in law whatever they may be, and if I do not reply I am guilty of an offence. If I do not sign a declaration which will estop me in the courts in the case of a prosecution from denying its truth, I am guilty of an offence under this order. How can the minister justify a power like that? I need only to state the case, I think, for every member of this house who believes in the fundamental .principles of British justice to see how flagrant this is. It is a fundamental principle of British justice that a man is innocent until1 he is proven guilty and that he may not be called upon to be a witness for the prosecution to prove his own guilt. That is a violation of a fundamental principle of British justice. This sort of legislation savours of certain sections of the prohibitory laws which were enacted by certain provincial legislatures in this country in days gone by. I do not think that anybody who reads it will approve it, and I ask the minister to have it amended so as to take this power away. To continue with this kind of procedure is a violation of the fundamental principles upon which British justice is founded, which is one of the things for which we are fighting to-day. This is the method of the gestapo. That may seem to be an extreme statement, but it is approximately correct. I do not know anything about the operation of this order. But I do object to these powers, and I think that the public ought to understand the powers of these inspectors and that the minister should review the whole situation.

In reply to questions already asked both in the house to-day and on the order paper the minister has referred only to the requests of the Manitoba government for amendments to the regulations to permit that province to pay a supplemental allowance to old age pensioners without its being charged as additional income. As the minister may know, when the government of Manitoba proposed to pay this additonal amount of $1.25 a month it was referred to by the government of Manitoba as the province's share of a proposed $5 increase, and both in the press and, I understand, in conferences that took place with people in Manitoba who were interested and called on the government, the impression was given that the Manitoba government would press this government to grant the payment of an additional $3.75 to all old age and blind pensioners in that province. I should like to know whether a request was made specifically for that amount of money, and, if so, whether any reply was given apart from that which the minister has already given to my questions on the order paper concerning the amending of the regulations.
One of the reasons why I should like to have a question such as that answered specifically is that it seems to me that the old people are unnecessarily being tossed back and forth from the provincial governments to the federal government. I listened veiy closely to the minister's statement last night, part of which he has repeated to-day, in which he declared that it is the view of the govern-

ment that the primary responsibility concerning the old1 age pensions rests with the provinces. I am sure he knows that in many, if not in all of the provincial legislatures of this country the very opposite position is stated with equal vigour and determination. That happened as I have already pointed out in the province of Manitoba, where the citizens pressed for an increase in the old age pension, and the provincial government said:	All
right, we will pay our share of a $5 increase, but the responsibility for the remainder rests with the federal government. I understand that even those provinces which have already granted a supplemental allowance of $5 a month have made it quite clear that in their view the primary responsibility for making any increase rests with this government. It seems to me that our old people and the young folks who are interested in them have cause to be concerned oyer this tossing of the responsibility from the provincial legislatures to this government and now back to the provincial legislatures. It would serve a good purpose if we could have a definite statement from the minister as to the correspondence and conversations passing between this government and, shall we say, the province of Manitoba, for example, to find out just where matters stand.
I agree heartily with the suggestion made a while ago-it has been made on several occasions, but was repeated this afternoon by the hon. member for Cumberland'-to the effect that this government would be well advised to approach the provincial governments with a view to getting together, not to find ways and means of how the responsibility can be passed from one government to the other, but to find ways and means of taking positive action to raise the amount of the pension.
I feel, too, that I must join with those who have already protested against referring to the necessity of sacrifice for the sake of the war effort by these old people over seventy who are being asked to live on $20 a month or less. We recognize the need for sacrifices in the community at large, but surely the place to put the burden is not on the shoulders of these old people. I am satisfied, like those who have spoken before me, that it would aid materially the morale of our fighting forces, and the feeling of the people in general that when this war is over, some of the better things we are fighting for are to be accomplished, if an increase could nowr be made in the amount paid to our old people. Therefore, I would ask, despite the kind of replies which have already been made by the minister, that he give us a more complete statement on the relations between this

government and the government of Manitoba in this matter, and indicate whether there is not some possibilty of the federal government trying to bring the various provincial governments together to discuss with this government, I say again, not ways and means of avoiding payment of an increase, but ways and means of taking positive steps to raise the amount now being paid.

Before the minister replies I wish to ask him something which bears on the same point, and arises out of letters received from overseas. Down through the years of the operation of the Old Age Pensions Act, extended to include pensions to certain of the blind, there has been a definite discrimination, as it appears to some, against old people who saved their pennies in the days of plenty and provided themselves with a small home; then, when the act became operative, they assigned these small homes in trust to the provincial gpvernments. I mention this matter because the minister has made his position perfectly clear, and I believe that considerable good will come out of this discussion. I hope that it will result in something being done on behalf of these old people who have taxes to pay. I trust that, in any new approach which may be made to the general problem, the minister will keep in mind the position of this large number of men and women who are living on $20 a month and are trying also to keep the taxes paid on their little properties, as they arc definitely committed to do.

The whole question was answered by the minister's speech in the House of Commons. I take it that the government do not intend to give any increase in old age pensions during the war.

I listened carefully to what the Minister of Finance said yesterday in regard to cost-of-living bonus, especially as applied to old age pensions, and he was quite emphatic. He said that the cost-of-living bonus depends primarily for its administration on the provincial governments, and that therefore the onus is upon them. Probably that is true from a legal point of view. But it must also be clearly understood that since the war started prices have tremendously increased. Responsibility for that cannot be placed upon the proyincial governments; it rests definitely upon the federal government, and especially upon the Minister of Finance, because under the War Measures Act he could have prevented the rise in prices. To a great degree he has done so, but whether he has succeeded or not is his responsibility. The provincial governments had absolutely no control in regard to the rise in the price of food or other necessaries; that came as a result of the war. I cannot see, therefore, how the minister can throw the entire responsibility for that increased cost upon the provincial governments.
It is true also that as these prices have increased the purchasing power of the $20 a month which the old age pensioners receive is reduced accordingly. If the provincial governments endeavour to offset that reduction by

an increase of $5 a month in the pension, as some provincial governments have, they must provide the money out of their own revenues. There has been an agreement with the federal government to forgo certain sources of revenue in that regard. Some of the provinces have a surplus, but the surplus has resulted only from the fact that nearly all provincial governments have economized in every possible way. They have eliminated a great many of their social services; they have restricted the construction of roads and other public works. In any event these surpluses are not so very large. For the minister merely to say that it is not the responsibility of the federal government and to leave it at that is not right. There is a moral obligation. When prices have increased and our old people are still expected to get along with the pittance formerly allowed them, it is a shame.
Let me give just one instance. The other jay I was at home out west for a few days when an elderly gentleman came to my home. He is sixty-seven years of age, and his wife is sixty-five. He had been farming in that district for forty years. Owing to one adversity after another the mortgage company had foreclosed and kicked him off his place and he was going to have to apply for old age pension. His wife is an invalid. To expect a man like that to exist on $25 a month, as it is in Alberta, is just not human.
The minister raised his hands in horror at the suggestion of some hon. members that something be done in this regard. He said we should not bring up a question of this kind now when we are so busy fighting a war, that he could not possibly carry on the tremendous financial burdens resulting from the conduct of the war and take care of all these other things as well. I think it is pretty well understood by all members that there have been tremendous increases in salaries since this war started. And some exceedingly large profits have been made. I suggest to the minister-I say this advisedly -that if he has only a limited amount of money to spend for this purpose, he should look around at some of the expenditures that are now being made and take a little bit away from those who are getting such tremendous amounts and redistribute it to old people who are really in need.
Not a great deal was said the other day about the increase in the price of meals. Restaurants were allowed to raise their prices to the extent of five cents for the beverage. I am not arguing at the moment whether that is a good or a bad thing, but it does result in a considerable profit to those concerned. It may have been fair enough if the minister had said that he would not allow that increased

price to benefit those individuals but would take it and apply it to old age pensions. That might be an extreme step to take, but when we realize that our war effort is being interfered with from the point of view of morale by our failure to take proper care of some of the old people in this country, especially those who have sons fighting in this war, I think some consideration should be given to the matter. May I add that the elderly gentleman who came to my house when I was out west had a son in the air force. The son came with him, and as they left my house the young fellow said to me, " Well, if this is the thing we are fighting for, I have not much encouragement in going to war.1'
This is a question that must be tackled. We cannot just idly say that it is not our responsibility. It is a national responsibility. The increased cost of living is due to the war and is a national problem. The minister and the house must realize that and take appropriate steps in the matter.

Will the minister
give serious consideration to a suggestion that has already been made by several hon. members, namely, that he call together representatives of the provinces in order to discuss with them this question of old age pensions? I had something to say on the question last evening and did not intend to take part in the discussion to-day, but as I entered the chamber a moment ago I heard the hon. member for South York make some references to the means test. I suggest to the minister and to the members of this house that in all cases where the amount of the pension or assistance given depends upon the economic circumstances of the individual, the means test should be broadened very considerably. People who have worked hard and tried to save something have found that what they have saved is a detriment to them instead of an asset, while people who have taken no care at all to provide for themselves when they became indigent or in difficult circumstances managed to obtain very easily whatever was coming to them. I know of men and women who have worked hard; who have raised families and tried to educate them to the best of their ability; who have tried to acquire a little home, and who may have a little money in the bank. Then when they can no longer work and have not enough to keep them, they find they must use up all their assets before they can get any assistance. This puts a premium on shiftlessness and makes it more difficult to get people to put something aside or to help themselves. Until that is changed people are not going to have a stake in this country that will be sufficient to induce them to try

US. To provide for the payment during the fiscal year 1942-43 to the Canadian National Railway Company (hereinafter called the National Company) upon applications approved by the Minister of Transport, made from time to time by the National Company to the Minister of Finance, and to be applied by the National Company in payment of the deficit (certified by the auditors of the National Company) in the operation of the Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals arising in the calendar year 1942-further amount required, $191,095.36.

I am
afraid I shall be obliged to take up some of the time of the committee to discuss certain matters arising out of this important item, and in doing so I shall review some of the history of the relationship between the province of Prince Edward Island and the confederation.
It will be recalled that Prince Edward Island was not one of the original provinces of the confederation. Although the conference was held at Charlottetown prior to 1867, Prince Edward Island did not come in until about 1873, and it came in under the provisions of an imperial order in council and the British North America Act. The order in council is dated June 28, 1873. It contains as a schedule an address to Her Majesty the Queen, which states the terms under which Prince Edward Island would enter confederation. Among those terms of union was the one which stated that the dominion government was to assume and defray all the charges in connection with certain services. It then goes on to enumerate certain specific services with which I am not particularly concerned, but it includes an efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers, to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, by the dominion, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the Intercolonial railway and the railway system of the dominion.
I submit that "efficient service" in that instance means modern, up-to-date service. That was the understanding upon which Prince Edward Island entered the union at that time. I believe it is fair to say that from 1873 down to 1915 that undertaking was not carried into fulfilment by any govem-

ment in Canada, especially with respect to winter transportation service. With regard to the summer service during that period, I do not think that in days gone by there was great complaint, having regard to the progress made in steam navigation and steam transportation. But I well remember as long as forty-nine years ago having seen with my own eyes passengers from Prince Edward Island having to traverse the strait of Northumberland1 in the old-time ice boat. I need only recall that period to indicate that at that time, at all events, there was no efficient method of transportation during the winter season between the little island province and the dominion.
The position stood thus until 1911 or thereabouts, when Sir Robert Borden, in the course of an election tour in that year, visited Prince Edward Island and gave the definite undertaking that if his part}'- were returned to power in the approaching election he would build and operate a steam ferry between the mainland and the island. I do not propose to refer to the demands for a tunnel, and things of that nature, because so far as I know they never got beyond the stage of academic discussions.
There is no doubt that as the result of the action of Sir Robert Borden, for the first time there was a moderately adequate fulfilment of the terms of confederation as set out in the address to Her Majesty the Queen in 1873. As the result of Sir Robert Borden's action the car ferry Prince Edward Island was built. That ferry operated with more or less success until about fifteen or twenty years ago

I have not the exact date, when she was more or less condemned, not as unseaworthy, but as inadequate for the service. The government of that day-I have forgotten which government it was-built the car ferry Charlottetown. I shall have something to say with respect to the loss of the Charlottetown later on. At the moment however suffice it to say that the island in my opinion had reasonably good transportation facilities from 1915 to 1941, first through the car ferry Prince Edward Island and then through the Charlottetown.
It is true that there was a great deal of objection to the cost of transportation. The car ferry was operated for the account of the dominion government by the then Department of Railways and Canals, now the Department of Transport, and the cost to the country was substantial. But any deficit in operation was a charge on the treasury by reason of the undertaking given in 1873, and I believe no one has raised any question with respect to that expenditure. In some years
