it has been larger, and in others smaller. But there has been a good deal of criticism of the rates charged for the transportation of freight, and at one time for the transportation of motor vehicles. From time to time there have been reductions in rates and some amelioration in conditions, because it must be	borne	in mind that the	cost oftransportation, aside from that borne by the treasury in the payment of deficits, in most cases came upon the shippers of products. In order	to get to	their markets	on the
mainland they were obliged-I believe it is fair to say this-to assume the cost of this extra transportation via the car ferry.
That condition was never properly righted, and the	time	came	when, owing	to theincrease in tourist traffic between the mainland and the island, the facilities were inadequate to	take	care	of the traffic	offering,
especially in the summer season. An effort was made to improve that condition when the Wood Island ferry was established1. It is now a matter of history and record that the efforts to establish that ferry were in a measure frustrated by reason of the fact that the vessels acquired for that purpose were, one after the other, requisitioned by the naval department. It was only within recent months that that service was established and maintained. No one has ever suggested that the establishment of the Wood Island ferry, or its predecessor the Hochelaga running from Pictou to the island, was anything more than supplementary to the main service.
In the summer of 1941 the Charlottetown was ordered to dry dock for her annual overhaul, and it is a matter of great misfortune that in that year she was lost off the coast of Nova Scotia. Since that time, in common with other hon. members, I have been asked by commercial interests and others in Prince Edward Island to lay before the government and the house the position of citizens in Prince Edward Island with respect to inadequacy of transportation facilities. I did so at great length on one occasion, and I have no apology for so doing. This season the situation has been aggravated by the severity of the weather conditions, and in the past several months the transportation facilities between the island and the mainland have been wholly inadequate. I think that is putting the matter quite mildly.
I wish to speak moderately on this subject; but I think it is inexcusable, if I may use that term, that we should be no further ahead than to have had a promise made by the minister in reply to a question asked by the senior member for Queens to the effect that plans were being prepared for a new car ferry, which would be built on an if, as and when basis.
That is not good enough for the province of Prince Edward Island. We have been told that it is impossible to get priorities for the
machinery and that no yard should be asked to build this new vessel. But there have been many occasions where moneys have been appropriated for peace-time activities which interfered with the war effort. I need but refer to the Montreal terminal, where millions have been spent on what is really a peace-time undertaking, while this situation on the island has been left unattended to.
I know that the government must have been presented with the representations which have been made from time to time by public bodies. The whole thing culminated this winter in a series of representations by public bodies, and the legislature of Prince Edward Island has gone on record unanimously as demanding that the rights of the citizens of that province, as outlined in the province's magna charta to which I have referred, shall be granted by the federal authorities. This has been followed up by a multitude of resolutions by nearly every board of trade on the island. Only recently there has been an exchange of correspondence between certain public and semipublic bodies in the province and the Prime Minister. I do not propose to place this on the record because it would take too long, but I do make a plea to the government to expedite the building of a new car ferry for the Northumberland strait.
I do not think all the avenues have been explored by the government or the Department of Transport to attain this end. I used to marvel at the fact that here was a province represented in this chamber by four members who support the administration. I am bound to say that so far as my own observations are concerned, up to this fourth session of this parliament the only public reference that has been made to this matter has been on two occasions. One was a question placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Queens, and the other was a speech made recently by the hon. member for Kings. I would have wished that these gentlemen had been a little more vocal with regard to this matter, especially since one of them sits on the treasury benches. I have no doubt that he will have something to say about it this afternoon.
The reason given-I shall not call it an excuse because I think there is some reason for it-is that the nation is at war. The nation is at war .but civilian life must go on. When we have an isolated island province such as Prince Edward Island it is the duty of the government to use every possible means within its power to see to it that a situation such as I have outlined is taken care of. There

is no question about the financial ability of the country to build this boat. That little province of 100,000 people has sent more volunteers per capita to the war than any other province.
Except Nova Scotia.

The two
provinces are in the same military district, and it is quite difficult to separate the voluntary enlistments of the two. Their record in voluntary enlistments for active service overseas has been magnificent. The little province of Prince Edward Island has no great industrial corporations within its boundaries and has practically no industry apart from agriculture, but it has gone over the top in the early days of every war loan campaign. That little province has been among the first of all provinces in its contributions to the Red Cross. In these days of grave national crisis that little province has exemplified the best there is of citizenship. I do suggest, moderately I hope, that Prince Edward Island has not had a fair deal at the hands of the federal government in connection with this transportation problem. I will not emphasize that any further.
There is something else to which I desire to refer to-night, namely, the loss of the ferry Charlottetown. I hold in my hand a copy of sessional paper 150, brought down in response to an order of this house made on February 8, on a motion by the hon. member for Cumberland, for a copy of the findings of Mr. Justice Archibald, with respect to the sinking of the ferry SS. Charlottetown off the coast of Nova Scotia in 1941. I make no apology

for referring to this matter this afternoon, because it is part and parcel of the subject matter with which I am dealing.
An investigation into the sinking of the Charlottetown was held in the months of December, 1941, and January and February, 1942, by Mr. Justice Archibald, as a wreck commissioner, assisted by certain naval officers and nautical assessors. Certain questions were submitted to that court.
I should preface my remarks in this connection by stating that the Charlottetown left Borden, Prince Edward Island, on the morning of June 16, 1941, on her way to Saint John, New Brunswick, for annual overhaul and repair. The finding of the court is that she was seaworthy at the time of her departure.
The findings of the court of inquiry indicate the type of ship the Charlottetown was. She had an indicated horse-power of 8,000; her speed was 15 knots, with eight boilers in use, and the dimensions of the ship are given.
It appears that when off Sambro light or near thereby she struck a rock or ledge, as a result of which she ultimately became a total loss. I will not go into the details of the findings, but I desire to read to the committee certain of the latter portion of the court's findings and I refer hon. members who have seen this report to paragraph 18:
18.	The ss. Charlottetown remained afloat after the striking a period of 32 hours and 13 minutes.
Please keep that in mind. Then paragraph 19.
19.	The vessel became a total loss by sinking on the evening of June 18, 1941, at 7.07 o'clock. At that time she was being towed by motor boats toward Port Mouton and sank in 16 fathoms of water-
In a certain latitude and longitude. Then mark this well. It is the finding of the court:
20.	The court is of opinion that the master either failed to realize the seriousness of the damage to the vessel and the necessity of immediate action to control the water and to secure assistance if the vessel was to be saved or that he was mistakenly confident that notwithstanding the damage he could take the vessel to a safe port. It is difficult to understand why the master did not within a very few minutes after the striking-
It was more than thirty hours after the striking that she actually sank. It goes on:
when she had reached deep water stop or even anchor the vessel and ascertain the damage suffered. It is apparent from the evidence t9ven particularly that of the chief engineer that the ship had suffered serious damage and that he had so advised the master. Notwithstanding this information there is no evidence that the master went below until the evening of June 17.

Supply-PJZ.I. Car Ferry
That was approximately twelve hours after the accident occurred. That is a factor to be kept in mind. The wreck commissioner proceeds to make this rather startling statement:
The method employed by the master in securing assistance seems to have been casual and inadequate. It must be observed that in the absence of a wireless system or any other method of communicating from the ship to the shore, it is difficult to understand why the ship's boat was not sent to shore immediately with the proper messages and instructions for assistance. Instead of doing so the master did not make any effort to establish communication with the shore until the vessel arrived at Little Hope buoy at 12.20 p.m. At that time a fisherman in a boat was at the buoy and to him the master gave a verbal message for transmission to the Canadian National Railways office at Moncton. This message he did not send. It was not until 4.30 o'clock in the afternoon of the 17th that a lifeboat left for the shore in charge of the first mate, who had with him the chief engineer, the chief steward and a crew of 17 men. When he reached shore that evening he sent a number of motor boats to the ship after having communicated with the general manager of the Canadian National Railways at Moncton and the district superintendent at Halifax and advising them of the ship's condition and the need for assistance, but notwithstanding this message it would seem that these officers must have had inadequate information as to the ship's peril; otherwise a greater effort would have been made in getting effective assistance to the distressed vessel without the lapse of a great length of time. It is difficult to understand why efforts were not made to get tugboats or other boats capable of giving assistance from the nearby ports of Shelburne, Loekport, Liverpool or Lunenburg. Having regard also to the condition of the vessel and the uncertainty as to the time of arrival of assistance it is difficult to understand why the vessel was not given in tow to motor boats during the night of June 17 or early on June 18 instead of waiting until 1.35 p.m. on the 18th.
I suggest that those findings of fact indicate that this boat could have been saved if the master had taken adequate measures. I desire to call the attention of the committee to finding 22:
In the opinion of the court the loss of the ss. Charlottetown resulted from the damage she suffered when she struck Devastation shoal and from the failure to take adequate measures to secure the safety of the ship after the striking and from the failure to obtain prompt and efficient assistance.
That responsibility was that of the master, and he wholly failed to assume that responsibility. Now listen to this. This is the summing up of the court:
The court is of opinion that the damage sustained by the ss. Charlottetown was caused by the wrongful act or default of her master, John Lefurgy Read in the following particulars:
(a)	He did not choose a proper or safe course in the weather conditions prevailing.
And reference is made to the answers given to questions 7, 8, 9 and 11.
(b)	His navigation of the vessel on this course was faulty and improper for the reasons given in the answers to questions 9, 11, 12 and 13.
I have not sketched the answers to those questions. I am contenting myself with giving the findings of the court of inquiry.
(c)	For the reasons given in the answers to questions 17 and 20 the master did not take the necessary and proper and adequate measures after the striking to ensure the safety of the vessel and to obtain assistance.
The court does not find that the damage and subsequent loss of the ss. Charlottetown was caused or contributed to by any other person or persons.
They go on to direct that the master's certificate be suspended for a period of six months.
There can be no doubt, I think, that the findings of the court were the findings of a legal and juridical tribunal. The master had the assistance of very able counsel. He was properly defended, and there should be no doubt in the minds of anybody that the master and the master alone was to blame.
Now what happened? The master's certificate was suspended. He was either dismissed or permitted to resign from his position with the Canadian National railway system. He was, however, given a pension of $154 a month, and he has been drawing it ever since.
What for?

I never understood that a man who was guilty of negligence, malfeasance, nonfeasance or any other kind of wrong feasance that one can imagine should be rewarded by being superannuated. I do not believe that is the law, and I see no justification for the payment of a pension to the master of this ship.
He was paid his full salary up to the time of the filing ol the commission's report.

Yes; ha was paid $400 a month up to the time of the findings of the wreck commission. A man is considered innocent until he is proved guilty, and there may be that justification for this proceeding, although it would appear to me that he ought to have been suspended by the management of the Canadian National railways immediately the ship was lost, if that was not done. That is what would have happened in connection with an ordinary commercial undertaking: a master having lost his ship, on the prima facie evidence submitted he would be suspended in the employment. Instead of that, this man was paid his full

Supply-P.E.I. Car Ferry

salary for several months after the ship was lost. And when he is found guilty of negligence, guilty of malfeasance, guilty of nonfeasance, he is rewarded by being allowed to resign, shall I say-I am not quite certain on that point-and given a pension of $154 a month; and I hear that he is petitioning the government to have the sentence of the court of inquiry reviewed so that he may have his certificate given back to him.
The first point I desire to make is, that through the action of the master the Charlottetown was lost; and my second point is that, as a result of the loss of the Charlottetown in the circumstances to which I have adverted, the people of Prince Edward Island have been deprived of adequate facilities for communication between their province and the mainland. It is no use to say, "Oh, you have had the Prince Edward Island." I think I am safe in saying that the Prince Edward Island was condemned for the service years ago; she was held as a stand-by during the time when the Charlottetown was undergoing repair, but she was considered to be wholly inadequate and not fit for the purpose during all the period Charlottetown was in operation. She was recommissioned, put on this route, and what has been the result? For days the island has been without proper communication. Hundreds of carloads of freight were accumulated on the docks. I have figures here showing what the situation was. Every public body in Prince Edward Island has protested, through the maritime board of trade, the Charlottetown board of trade, the Summerside board of trade, and other boards of trade, and through the legislature itself. Most of them consider that improper treatment-I will use no stronger term-has been handed out to them by reason of the failure of the governent to provide adequate transportation facilities as required by the compact of confederation, in which they were partners.
I have no desire to carry on this debate at inordinate length. I could go into the matter in much more detail. But if I serve no other useful purpose than to call attention on the floor of this chamber to the situation which exists, and to obtain from the ministry some undertaking of a character which will tend to alleviate the situation, I shall feel amply repaid for any effort I have made, and it will redound to the benefit of the people of Prince Edward Island. I earnestly implore the minister to deal with this matter. The people of Prince Edward Island have been good enough to accept him as their representative in this house. I know he will agree with me that he owes a corresponding duty to them to

do anything and everything to remedy a situation which he knows as well as I do exists. I invite him to tell the committee exactly what the proposals of the government are in that regard.
I know he will say that, on account of the exigencies of the war, the government has not been able to get another vessel in place of the one which was lost. I agree at once that it is exceedingly difficult to find a ship of the type required for this service, but I certainly believe that there should have been more adequate provision than was made in attempting to recommission the Prince Edward Island ferry.
Therefore, without desiring to take any more of the time of the committee, and hoping I have been reasonably moderate in the statements I have made, I invite the minister to tell the people of Prince Edward Island through the medium of this committee exactly what the government proposes to do and when they may expect that proper communication of a modern character will be renewed between the island and the mainland.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. E. MICHAUD (Minister of Transport) :
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this committee took recess at six o'clock the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) had just concluded an appeal on behalf of residents of Prince Edward Island on account of existing transportation conditions between the island and the mainland owing to unfortunate circumstances to which I shall refer a little later. The hon. member made many exaggerated statements, of which three are out-, standing. The first was that no government since the entry of Prince Edward Island into confederation had been true to the population of the island, in the matter of providing adequate transportation services between the island and the mainland. The second was that the present ferry service is inadequate; and the third, that the people of the island were left isolated as a result of lack of attention on the part of the government in providing proper ferry facilities. I shall present a few facts and leave it to the intelligence of hon. members to judge whether governments in the past have been delinquent in their duty to the island and in the fulfilment of one of the conditions under which Prince Edward Island1 joined confederation.

Supply-PH.I. Car Ferry
As stated by the hon. gentleman, on June 26, 1873, an order in council was passed whereby Prince Edward Island was made a part of the Canadian confederation. In that order in council there was this provision:
Efficient steam service for the conveyance of mails and passengers to be established and maintained between the island and the mainland of the dominion, winter and summer, thus placing the island in continuous communication with the intercolonial railway and the railway system of the dominion.
As stated by the hon. member, from that time to 1916 the facilities for transporting mails, passengers and freight were maintained by private companies or corporations operating ferries in the summer between Summer-side. Prince Edward Island, and Point du Chene, New Brunswick, and in the winter between Georgetown, Prince Edward Island, and Pietou, Nova Scotia. During that period extending from 1873 to 1916 these services were provided by private companies subsidized by the dominion treasury.
In 1913 the dominion government decided to provide more adequate service. First, I should say that up to 1913 there was no demand for any car ferry service, for two obvious reasons: first, because there was no possibility of moving freight cars or passenger cars between the island and the mainland because the railway on the island was of a different gauge from that of the mainland. Second, there was no demand for transportation of automobiles to and from the island, because prior to that time the laws of the province prohibited the operation of motor vehicles on the island. But then a change of policy took place; in 1911 and 1912 the government decided to change the gauge of the railway on the island and bring it to standard gauge, and the .provincial laws were relaxed permitting the use of automobiles.
A ferry service was instituted which would move railway cars and automobiles. The construction of a combined passenger and car ferry which would serve in all seasons was decided upon. It was completed in 1916 and put into service between Charlottetown and Pietou until the completion of the terminal facilities. The Prince Edward Island car ferry was built by the government for that purpose at a cost of $2,280,000 and put into service.
In 1926 the Duncan commission made a report recommending that still better facilities should be provided. Those recommendations were implemented. In 1929 the then government decided that a larger and better car
ferry should be provided, and voted an appropriation of $3,500,000. In Hansard for the session of 1929 I read this item at page 3078:

Railways-Canadian Government Railways- to provide for additional ear ferry and facilities for car ferry service between the mainland and Prince Edward Island, $3,500,000.
Mr. Manion: Would the minister explain this item?
Mr. Dunning:	It will be remembered that
one of the features of the report of the Duncan commission related to the necessity for improved ferry accommodation for Prince Edward Island. I need not go into the reasons therefor, because they have been discussed in the house on many occasions. Last year an amount was appropriated to start the work. In the meantime a careful investigation has been made with respect to the matter, so far as time and facilities would permit, by the Canadian National authorities on behalf of the department. There was a suggestion many years ago that money might be saved and better facilities afforded at lower annual charges if a tunnel were constructed between the mainland and the island. I thought it desirable to have the old reports in that connection looked up and checked by the engineers in the light of present conditions in order to see, facing as we were a considerable expenditure in any event, what were the economics of the tunnel suggestion. Another suggestion was that a causeway might be built across to the island from the mainland.
Mr. Manion: What is the distance?
Mr. Dunning:	The shortest distance across
is nine miles. The result of the investigation during the year reveals that a tunnel would cost to-day in the neighbourhood of $40,000,000. Hon. gentlemen will understand that that is not a detailed estimate, because considerable engineering work would be necessary to determine the sub-aqueous conditions.
This shows that in 1929 the government took some steps to provide adequate facilities for the service between the island and the mainland. Then	between	1929 and	1930	acontract was let	for the	construction of	acar ferry, and on March 20, 1930, the late Mr. Woodsworth	asked a	question	in thisregard, which is	reported	at page	777	of
Hansard for that year:
Mr. J. S. Woodsworth (Winnipeg North Centre):	Is it a fact that the building of the
car ferry for Prince Edward Island has been let to the province of Quebec? I have a protest from Halifax stating that the wages in Quebec are much lower than in Halifax.
Hon. Charles A. Dunning (Minister of Finance):	Speaking for the Minister of Railways, I can only say that the contract for the Prince Edward Island ferry was let to the lowest tenderer. My recollection is that it is the Davie Shipbuilding Company of Levis. Quebec, and, of course, the contract will contain the usual protective clauses with respect to labour.
So much for the construct ion of that car ferry, which was named the Charlottetown. It was put into service in 1931, and from that
Supply-P.E.I. Car Ferry

time until 1941 served the purpose for which it was built. In June, 1941, it was considered advisable to have considerable repairs and overhauling done to that boat, and it was ordered to Saint John for that purpose. As we all know, on June 17 it struck a rock and foundered, and it is now at the bottom of the sea.
From 1916 or 1917 to the present time the car ferry has been operated by what was at first the Canadian government railways and later the Canadian National Railways. Prior to 1938 the accounts were not segregated from those of the Canadian National Railways, but in 1938 they were segregated and the ferry continued to be operated for the Canadian government by the Canadian National Railways. From 1933 to 1942 inclusive the total deficit on the operation of the car ferry amounted to 83,959,164.99, and during the year 1942 the deficit amounted to $591,095.36. These deficits do not include provision for the depreciation of vessels or interest on the investment, with the exception of interest on a small portion of that investment which was financed by the Canadian National, amounting to $388,255.74. Prior to the end of 1942 the country's investment in the Prince Edward Island car ferry and terminals amounted to $6,953,681.33.
Does the minister suggest that an operating deficit is an investment? Whoever wrote that brief does not understand proper accounting.
I never suggested that.
That was what the minister said.

No. I said the deficit did not include provision for the depreciation of vessels or interest on the investment; that is, interest on the investment was not charged against the deficit for the year. The details of the investment are as follows: terminals at Cape Tormentine, $2,103,451.85, and at Borden, $2,840,288.82. The investment in the ferry Prince Edward Island amounts to $815,795.22. As I stated, the cost of the ferry Charlottetown was $2,189,145.44, less insurance recovered amounting to $995,000. Therefore the total capital cost is the figure I mentioned previously, $6,953,681.33.

I understand that the
Charlottetown was insured, and the minister has said that $995,000 was recovered. When the vessel was sunk, did the government abandon all its rights to the underwriters of the insurance?
Yes.
Is there no possibility of the government getting any part of the salvage now?

No; that has been investigated, and it has been found that it would not be possible to salvage anything with the exception of what could be obtained from the insurance.
Since June, 1941, the service has been maintained by the ferry Prince Edward Island. It has been claimed that this boat is very old, that it has been condemned, and so on. My information is that the Prince Edward Island was in commsission continuously from 1916 to 1931, and was maintained in very good repair. After the Charlottetown was put in service, the Prince Edward Island was kept as a stand-by. Every year it was inspected by the steamship inspection board, and two or three years after the Charlottetown had been put in commission and had proven satisfactory, the Prince Edward Island was overhauled at considerable expense. Since that time it has been regularly inspected and kept in commission. In the summer of 1941 it was put in service between Cape Tormentine and Borden. During that period the service has been maintained continuously, except for three or four days last winter when either the rudder or the propeller was cracked. One Saturday the part was taken to a foundry in Charlottetown and repaired over Saturday night and Sunday, and I am told that on that occasion two and a half days were lost.
Does the minister regard the present service as adequate?
The present service, yes. I certainly regard the service of the Prince Edward Island as adequate for present needs.
Is that the view of hon. members from Prince Edward Island?

I think it is. I have
no doubt of it, because with the exception of two or three days the car ferry has been operating, and has been transporting all the freight and passengers offered.

Is that
adequate information, because I have reports to show that at one time there were 100 loaded cars awaiting transshipment, and that those cars were held up.

I have not that information. In 1942 the Prince Edward Island made 3,886 trips, while the Charlottetown in 1940 had made only 2,772. The following is a table which will show some information with

After June, 1941, and during 1942, repairs on the Prince Edward Island were made to the extent of $102,663.52. In the summertime one of the Scotias operating from Canso was assigned as a stand-by to the Charlottetown. In the wintertime there was no other car ferry available on the north American continent, and for that reason provisions were made to detail an icebreaker to take care of passengers and mail, in the event of an. emergency.
During this last winter?
Yes.
Was there any icebreaker there?

Not in attendance all the time, because the icebreakers were busy cutting ice in the gulf. But an icebreaker was to be assigned whenever necessity arose. And during the very short time the car ferry was disabled it was not thought absolutely necessary to send an icebreaker for two days to that 'locality.
As a matter of fact no icebreaker was there at all last winter.

There was no icebreaker as a stand-by, because last winter icebreakers in the gulf of St. Lawrence were very busy. They did work in that vicinity.
I admit, however, it would be much better if we could have a second car ferry as a stand-by all the time. That was the intention of the government, and it still is. I submit that all governments since confederation have done their duty by providing a most adequate service. From confederation to 1916 they gave the service the people of the island wanted; and I have no information that they asked for any service other than the one which they received, and which was subsidized.
With the advent of modern transportation, improved railways, tourist traffic and automobile traffic, a modern boat was provided. Ten years later, with improved transportation facilities, and greater demands, another boat was provided, with the idea of having a stand-by. Since the accident to the Charlottetown the whole north American continent has been searched for a car ferry to act as a stand-by to the Prince Edward Island, but it has been impossible to find any. I believe that must be admitted.
The question of building a new car ferry has been considered. Under present-day conditions we are led to believe that a new ferry would cost at least $4,500,000. Since the loss of the Charlottetown marine architects have been working on plans, with a view to designing a new car ferry, with improvements of a 1943 rather than a 1916 type. For this purpose the most modern icebreakers have been inspected.
Not so long ago we were informed that what was supposed to be the acme of perfection in icebreakers, namely, the Stalin, was on the Pacific coast. We dispatched marine architects to inspect that boat, to see if they could find anything which would improve on Canadian designs developed thus far. I am happy to say that upon their return they said they found nothing on that boat which they did not already know, or that Canadian science had not already explored.
With regard to the duty of the federal government toward Prince Edward Island in connection with supplying a ferry service it is my belief that this matter has been given careful attention by all governments and, up to the time of the loss of the Charlottetown the people of the island received1 very good service. They had a stand-by, the Prince Edward Island, in the event of accident.
In view of the fact that it is difficult at this time to use shipyards for building boats of a type other than those used for war purposes exclusively, I submit that the service now being provided is adequate to meet the requirements of the traffic. I agree that it would not meet the requirements in case of a major accident.
With regard to the future, let me say that I sympathize as much as the hon. member for York-Sunbury with the good people of the island. I agree that their contribution to the war effort has not been excelled in any other part of the country. The mainland entered into a contract with them at the time of confederation, and that contract will be fulfilled. They must be given the best service possible in the matter of ferry transportation.
Supply-PE.I. Car Ferry

and we intend to give it. The government has authorized the Department of Transport to take every means possible to provide a modern ear ferry, and we have been authorized by order in council to spend up to $3,000,000 during the present year. It is estimated that this car ferry will cost at least $4,500,000, based on the cost of the Charlottetown in 1930, plus the increases in cost of material and labour, and plus the added improvements that would be made in a new boat.
There is nothing in the estimates for that.

I agree that there is nothing in the estimates now before the house, but that has been authorized by order in council. The best naval architects in Canada-I believe it is the firm which designed the Charlottetown -have been at work preparing plans for the new ferry. When the plans and designs are completed we shall have to find a shipyard that will be willing to undertake the building of a car ferry of this type. This is not the standard type of car ferry. I believe my information is correct that all shipyards in Canada are now tooled up for building boats required for war purposes, either cargo boats or defence boats of one kind or another. In order to build a boat of this type it would be necessary to take some shipyard off its present work. That would mean giving priority over war requirements. Nevertheless, as soon as the plans are completed, we shall call for tenders for the building of a ferry boat of the type required for this service.
This will take some time. It will depend upon the architects and upon the shipyards now building ships for war purposes. I think the people of Prince Edward Island understand the difficulties under which we are labouring. It is not a question of policy; it is not a question of funds; it is simply a question of the government appropriating the materials and labour without interfering too much wdth the war effort in the way of constructing cargo boats, minesweepers, corvettes and other defence boats. I think that is about all I have to say for the moment. Let me repeat that nothing has been left undone which it was possible to do in order to replace the boat which was lost in June, 1941.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury was critical of the government because Captain Read, the master of this boat, was censured by Mr. Justice Archibald, who acted as investigator.
I did not criticize the government about that; I was merely stating a fact.

The hon. member criticized the government because Captain Read had been given a pension after having been found guilty of negligence. It must be understood that Captain Read was an old official of the Canadian National Railways. Before being employed by the Canadian National Railways in the operation of this ferry, he had been employed by the government. At the time of the accident, as I say, he was an employee of the Canadian National Railways, and he was given charge of the Prince Edward Island up until the date of the findings of Mr. Justice Archibald on February 25, 1942, when he was suspended by the Canadian National Railways. Captain Read had been a contributor to the Intercolonial and Prince Edward Island railways employees' provident fund. This is not a government pension fund; it is a fund created by the employees and administered by them.
And by the management.
Supervised by the management. Under the rides and regulations of that fund Captain Read was entitled to a pension based on the amount of his contributions.

Would the
ordinary employee of the railway, an ordinary trackman, have that privilege? Cases have come to my knowledge where trackmen have been dismissed for dereliction of duty and have been denied the benefits of the provident fund to which they had contributed for years.
No.
Oh, yes.
That has been my experience.

My information is that the question of a pension to Captain Read was investigated thoroughly by the administrators of the fund and by the officials of the Canadian National Railways. The case was submitted to the legal department of the railways, and they were told that they had to pay the pension to Captain Read.

That is
hearsay; has the minister that opinion with him?
I have not any writing before me, but that is the information I got from the officials of the Canadian National railways.

That should aPPl}' to everybody who has been dismissed. They should all be entitled to a pension when they have contributed to the fund.

I think it depends upon the rules and regulations under which the fund is administered. There are several factors which enter into the matter and which, I am told, have been considered carefully by the administrator's of the fund and by the officials of the Canadian National railways who have supervision of the fund, and by their legal department. The situation is that Captain Read is no longer in the employ of the Canadian National railways; he is retired and is drawing a pension.

My hon. friend the member for York-Sunbury has taken some time to deal with this matter. One of the suggestions he made was that the members from Prince Edward Island had not been sufficiently vocal, to use. his own words, about this matter. Speaking for myself I do not conceive it to be my duty to rise in my place in the house and speak on a question regarding which I have the fullest information, and regarding which my energy has been devoted in trying to get action rather than talking about it.
We have not had much action yet.
If my hon. friend will content himself for a minute-
I will do that.

-I wish to say to my hon. friend and to the committee that the members from Prince Edward Island, including myself, have been expending our energy and our efforts in endeavouring to see if something can be done and in seeing the appropriate ministers and the Canadian National railway regarding the matter, rather than making speeches in the house for the benefit of our constituents.
That would be all right if you got any action.

If my hon. friend will still content himself for a minute or two, I wonder whether he is really serious in his urgings in this matter, or is he just doing it for the purpose of making a little cheap political capital?
Order.

I know, but my hon. friend is interrupting all the time. It seems to me that he is unduly anxious in this matter. I am just as anxious as he is, as I propose to demonstrate, and I have been anxious a good deal longer and have done a good deal more in connection with it, along with my colleagues, than my hon. friend has done. He has contented himself with making speeches.
We have to be realistic in this matter. We have had to face a situation which existed, and not some imaginary peace-time situation which my hon. friend has in mind. We have had to realize there was a war on, and I do not think my hon. friend did realize that when he made- the speech he did this afternoon and advocated the getting of a new ferry for Prince Edward Island immediately. If he knows anything about shipping he knows that every one of the united nations is engaged in producing as fast as it can cargo vessels and escort vessels. Every shipyard in Canada is busy in connection with that, as also is every shipyard in the United States. Every available piece of shipping is being taken. Ships are even being taken off the beach and having sails put on them to provide transportation.
My hon. friend, I presume, thinks he can make some sort of appeal to the people of Prince Edward Island by suggesting that we empty one of those berths now so busily engaged and put a car ferry into construction there which would take perhaps a year or a year and a half to build, and in the meantime we would lose the building of ten cargo vessels or eight escort vessels. I wish to say that the people of Prince Edward Island are not to be caught by that sort of thing. I am prepared to go to them at any time and tell them the situation, instead of making speeches in the house, and I and my colleagues have told them the situation. When my hon. friend talks of patriotism he does not know half as much about the patriotism of the people of Prince Edward Island as I do from my position. From the beginning of this war Prince Edward Island has been excelled in recruiting by no other province, not even by my native province which was mentioned by the hon. member for Cumberland this afternoon. The people of Prince Edward Island have gone over the to-p also in connection with every victory loan campaign and every Red Cross drive That little island contains a population of less than half that of the city of Ottawa, and yet it has overseas at the present time two artillery batteries, a squadron of the Prince Edward Island Light Llorse, a company in the North Nova Scotia Highlanders, medical units and personnel, signallers and men in every arm of the service. It has on this side the Prince Edward Island Highlanders who have been on a long and arduous tour of duty in Newfoundland. It has a veterans' guard company. I know something about the people of Prince Edward Island
Supply-P.E.I. Car Ferry

and their patriotism, and I know their patriotism can, be appealed to when we are in the midst of great difficulties with respect to the shipping situation.
I wish to say here and now-this may not be an example of cabinet solidarity-that I do not regard the ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland as adequate, having regard to what we should like to have in the way of modern facilities. But I do say, that in the light of all the needs at the present time I am sure that the people of Prince Edward Island will endeavour to do their best, provided that they are assured that we are doing everything we possibly can to meet the situation.
Let me tell my hon. friend what we have done. The programme when that terrific disaster occurred, and it was a terrific disaster, was to endeavour to see if we could not find some sort of stand-by for the present.
I went everywhere making inquiries. I did not know much about shipping, and it was a citizen of Prince Edward Island who suggested to me that we ought to go on the west coast of the United States and try to get a boat at Los Angeles or San Francisco. I took that up with Mr. Vaughan at the time. I wrote him and asked him about it, and he told me that he had already been making inquiries to see if he could find any other boat to act as a stand-by. They found a boat called the Sacramento and sent marine architects to look her over. They found that on two counts she would not do: (1) it was very doubtful if she would stand the seas coming around, and (2) she would be only a summer boat anyway; she could not stand the ice. Then they looked at a boat at Milwaukee, and the same situation existed with regard to her. These boats are not used in ice. My hon. friend a minute ago had the idea that we use an icebreaker between Tormentine and Borden.
The minister referred to that. I never did.

The Prince Edward Island and the Charlottetown are icebreakers, with a superstructure on top for carrying cars and passengers. With these boats that were looked at in the United States you would have to have an icebreaker. There was another boat at Detroit owned by the Canadian National Railways, but it was impossible to get her through the locks without cutting her in two. The same situation existed in regard to another boat at Cobourg.
I did not make any. speeches. I wish to give my hon. friend the attitude I adopted as

a member of this government in writing to Mr. Vaughan about the possibility of getting a boat for a stand-by. Here is what I said:
I think we must proceed on the basis that a new boat is indispensable. The Charlottetown was evidently regarded as imperatively necessary when she was built, even though they had the Prince Edward Island. The need now is very much more vital and much more acute than then. The Charlottetown will have to be replaced, and if the materials were obtainable a new boat would be under way now. Consequently, a fill-in is necessary because a new boat is necessary. There may have to be a good deal of extra expense in order to furnish that fill-in, but I don't consider that engineers are in a position to say, as Messrs. German and Company apparently have, that a certain cost would be prohibitive. The cost is not prohibitive if the boat is required. I think that the war is really just beginning and that we have to think in terms of expansion. It follows that we must have a new boat and a substitute until a new boat can be obtained.
I cannot content myself with the fact that the Prince Edward Island may possibly or even probably be able to carry on. We must provide the best insurance we can against the possibility of her not carrying on or of her proving inadequate for the service.
That is the position I took then-, and that is the position I take to-day. I did not make any speeches in the house. Here is the position after months of rigorous examination. I was talking to Mr. Vaughan to-night. The technical experts of the Canadian National Railways have been sent all over the continent to find a boat which would be a suitable stand-by, and they have been unable to find one so far. Shipping is at a terrific premium. It is as scarce as the proverbial hen's teeth. While we want to have that stand-by, we have not a standi-by at the present time, and what is the alternative? The measure which needs to be taken is the building of a new boat, and the building of a new boat as soon as possible. But in the meantime, what? The situation is simply this, that we have there icebreakers not far away. If there were a serious breakdown in connection with that service, in the wintertime,
I say to the people of Prince Edward Island as I say to this house, what you would have to do is to have an icebreaker there and cargo boats in order to carry the cargo. But we also have a stand-by at Canso in the shape of the second boat there, and I am told that technical experts find that, of all the boats available, the Scotia is probably the best of the .very limited supply the government has as a stand-by in connection with that service. But this is not the fault of the government, or of hon. members from Prince Edward Island, or of this house. That is the situation we are in because there is a war on. I have an assurance from my colleagues the Minister

Supply-P.E.I. Car Ferry
of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of Transport that icebreakers would be made available and that we would have a stand-by if necessary.
This is not a situation which is desirable, or one that I want to see continue. If there is anything which can be done to improve that situation, I am anxious and I am sure my colleagues are anxious to do it. But we have to be realistic and understand what the situation is.
So much with regard to the winter. As regards summer conditions, the situation is very much easier, because there is the Scotia I or the Scotia II. I believe it is the Scotia I which is a- stand-by for the service between Mulgrave and Point Tupper and the service between Borden and Prince Edward Island; that is, if the necessity should arise, but we hope it will not.
Does my hon. friend who speaks of a boat twenty-nine years old realize that the Lady Grey is forty-eight years old, and that she was put in service again this year as an icebreaker? That indicates what we are up against in the matter of shipping. Prince Edward Island has done magnificent work: she has run this whole year at an average of better than ten trips a day, over eight miles each, through ice and ice floes and under bad conditions. Some trips have taken as long as eight hours. She has done splendid work. We put in oil-burning boilers this year, the last of them having been completed very recently, and they have made a tremendous improvement.
As has been said, that boat served from 1915 to 1931. I think I am correct in saying that that is when the new boat was put on. There had been only one boat up to that time. We are now back in the same situation with an older boat. I realize that this is so, and what we are tiying to do is to provide the best stand-by possible. I assure the people of Prince Edward Island that this will be done.
With regard to security, I have discussed that with my colleagues the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and the Minister of National Defence for Air, and I am assured that everything will be done that can possibly be done with the equipment that is available to afford security for that boat on that particular run.
As an extra precaution, as a matter of stand-by, the Prince Edward Island members and I have advocated to my colleague the Minister of Transport that, to take care of a temporary breakage in connection with that boat, we should have at Prince Edward Island either a marine slip or a floating dock where repairs may be made, and whereby two disadvantages will be avoided-delays on the
boat being taken to some other port for repairs, and the risks attendant on a voyage of that kind. That matter is under consideration right at this moment. We found the value of such an arrangement at the very time my hon. friend spoke about it. I am not sure whether it was repairs to the propeller or the rudder which took three days; but when a breakdown occurred we found the value of having a machine shop and a place where repairs could be made right on Prince Edward Island. The boat was taken to Charlottetown and was back on the run in about two and a half days. If we have a floating dock and a marine slip there, it will be possible to make all repairs on the spot with comparatively little loss of time.
That is the situation with regard to the Prince Edward) Island ferry. It is not by any means an ideal one; nobody realizes that more than I do. I hope no one in this chamber or anywhere else will suggest that the island members have not done all they can about it. If my hon. friend or anyone else can tell me of a boat tucked away in a bureau drawer somewhere, any boat which we can beg, borrow or steal, we shall have it. The fact is that such a boat just does not exist at the present time as far as the technicians of the Canadian National Railways can find, and they have put marine architects on that very search.
One word more. I want the committee to realize what the shipping situation is in Canada and in the world. I cannot go into details, but I assure hon. members that nobody knows better than I do how tight the shipping supply is for the movement of materials and men. I will go as far as to say that to-night on the docks in Canada a lot of equipment is awaiting shipment to points where it would be extremely valuable in the war in which we are all engaged. The people of Prince Edward Island are not going to ask that a berth, now filled with a cargo boat which can carry that stuff, shall be vacated for the purpose of building a ferry which will take, under present conditions, a year or two build. The situation may change. We hope that, on account of the drive which is on, in Canada and the United States particularly, for the building of cargo ships, a berth may be released before very long. But I must make it clear that the drive is on in 1943. I want the house to remember that, and I know that the people of Prince Edward Island, who have shown their loyalty in the matter of everything which has to do with the carrying on of the war, will recognize it as well. In connection with the building of a ferry of this sort, it is not simply a matter of providing a

Supply-PJ2.I. Car Ferry

berth and constructing the hull. There is much more than that. To-night, five hundred different shops across Canada are engaged in the manufacture of components for shipping. Those are . standard mass production components, in order that all may be put in the same kind of ship. When you have to divert three or four or five shops to the making of turbines for a particular kind of ferry, such as this, and the manufacture of what may be special propellers, steering gear and instruments, you cut- down perceptibly the output of the escort boats and cargo vessels which are needed in the battle of the Atlantic, the biggest battle of 1943.
I assure the people of Prince Edward Island and the members of this committee that we shall expedite in every way we possibly can the building of a ferry which will be adequate, in the words of my hon. friend, to meet their needs; a ferry better than the Charlottetown, although I do not think I need have much hesitation in saying that she was probably the best ferry of her kind in the world.
The people of Prince Edward Island rely on us to do our level best in connection with this matter. They want to be assured and they have a right to be assured that we are doing our level best. We rely on them to show the same loyalty and the same willingness to inconvenience themselves, to make some sacrifice if necessary, as they have done in connection with other phases of our war effort. I believe that the reliance and dependence of one on the other will be quite sufficient, and will be fully justified.
One thing more. This is a matter which has to do with more than exclusively the people of Prince Edward Island. I regard this ferry service as a national undertaking- I mean exactly what I say-national because promised in the days gone by with regard to transportation services, that is that reasonable transportation was to be given for the island itself; national in that Prince Edward Island as the cradle of confederation had a right to some consideration with respect to transportation. It is national in more senses than that, because there are to-day two schools of the air training plan on Prince Edward Island and another is to be completed before very long. For these services it is just as essential as any other national undertaking and just as much a part of our war effort. Therefore I hope that this committee will believe that the government is fully alive to the necessity for providing the very best transportation facilities possible, in view of the difficulties that surround us in these realistic times. We are fully alive to

that, not simply on account of the interests of a particular section of the community, but because we believe it is a national undertaking and desirable in the interest of bringing to the best fruition the national effort in which we are all engaged.

Just a brief word in reply. I have no apology to make for having brought this subject before the committee. The publicity which will be given to the discussion here this afternoon and this evening wili be of great benefit. I agree with the latter part of the minister's remarks, that this is a national undertaking and one which must be brought to fruition at the earliest possible moment. I do not agree with his colleague, and I am delighted to find myself in agreement with the Minister of National Defence.
It is only a matter of opinion.
No; it is a matter of fact. Every public body in Prince Edward Island has condemned the service as inadequate. The legislature has unanimously passed a resolution to that effect.
"Adequacy" 1ms to be judged by what one can do.

That is a factor. But the fact remains that the service is inadequate. I find myself in agreement with the great mass of the people of Prince Edward Island in that respect.
With respect to providing a second ship, the minister has painted a picture with respect to the shipping position of which I think we are all pretty well aware. But I suggest this: This ship was built in the Davie shipyard. The building of a shipyard in itself is not a very important consideration with respect to the construction of this ship. I am told by those who know that the capital cost of constructing a shipyard suitable for the building of a vessel similar to the Charlottetoiun would not be great. I admit that there are other considerations which would have militated and may militate now if immediate action is not taken for the early construction of this ship; that is, getting the necessary machinery and priority.
The Charlottetown was lost in June, 1941, nearly two years ago. We have not yet reached the stage of even having planned for a new vessel. That is not good enough. The minister was right in his first conclusion when he wrote that letter to Mr. Vaughan in April, 1942, just

Supply-P.E.I. Car Ferry
under a year ago, saying that a new ship would have to be built. There is no doubt as to that.
I have no apology to make to this committee 'or the nation or the people of Prince Edward Island for having advocated publicly their interest on the floor of this house, and I hope the time will never come when I shall fail to do my duty as a member of this house to any part of this dominion.

This afternoon my hon. friend Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury) who has just taken his seat made reference to P.C. 1774, namely, the enforcement order dealing with the wage stabilization policy. If I remember correctly, he applied the term "gestapo" to it and said that these inspectors were going to give the employers of this country the third degree. I do not think my hon. friend was serious when he made those remarks.
I said, if 1 remember correctly, that it savoured of the gestapo.
That is an audit.

Well, they go in and
check the payrolls, and in checking the payrolls they can see whether an employer is paying the correct cost-of-living bonus, and report back to the regional boards and the national board. I thought when we laid down that policy that was the most economical and soundest thing to do. It was far better than having two sets of inspectors dealing with almost identical matters.
I was amazed at my friend taking the very strong attitude he did this afternoon. He said:
I do not think anybody who reads it will approve it, and I ask the minister to have it amended so as to take this power away. To continue with this kind of procedure is a violation of the fundamental principles upon which British justice is founded, which is one of the things for which we are fighting to-day.
I have no quarrel with my hon. friend standing for the principles which have made the British people what they are, and enabled them to make the contribution they have to the science of government. But when my friend refers to these regulations as gestapo and third degree procedures I might remind him that he voted for identically the same regulations under the unemployment insurance bill in 1940.
I probably did not know about it.

Oh, my hon. friend is
not as innocent at that. I should like to read into the record the language; it is almost identical except for one or two necessary changes, because one deals with a wage stabilization policy and the other with unemployment insurance. This is section 73 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, chapter 44, statutes of 1940:
73.	Any person authorized by the commission to act as an inspector shall, for the purpose of the execution of this act, have power to do all or any of the following things, namely:
(a)	to enter at all reasonable times any premises or place, other than a private dwelling house not being a workshop, where he has reasonable grounds for supposing that any insured persons are employed;
(b)	to make such examination and inquiry as may be necessary for ascertaining whether the provisions of this act are complied with in any such premises or place;
(c)	to examine orally, either alone or in the presence of any other person, as he thinks fit, with respect to any matters under this act, every person whom he finds in any such premises or place, or whom he has reasonable cause to believe to be or to have been an employed person, and to require every such person to be so examined, and to sign a declaration of the truth of the matters in respect of which he is so examined;
(d)	to exercise such other powers as may be necessary for carrying this act into effect.
74.	The occupier of any such premises or place and any other person employing any employed person, and the servants and agents of any such occupier or other person and any such employed person shall furnish to any inspector all such information and shall produce for inspection all such registers, books, cards, wage sheets, records of wages and other documents as the inspector may reasonably require.
Then the penalty clause is section 75'. I think my hon,. friend will agree with me that

the inspectors charged with this responsibility will not undertake the third degree of any person in Canada. As the responsible minister I say I would not stand for it for five minutes if the facts were brought to my attention. I read that into the record just because I did not want it to be understood in the country that the Department of Labour had been turned into a gestapo, when the regulations to which my hon. friend referred were copied almost exactly from a statute passed iby a government of which he was an honoured member.

I have not the order in council before me, but I do not believe any order in council, containing a provision like that, ought to be put through in the secrecy of cabinet council. If a public statute is put through, parliament is aware of it; publicity is given to it, and if it passes, well and good. I do not recall the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act; I do not think we examined them here on the floor of this house section by section.

speechtext: Yes, we did.
Were they not before a special committee?

speechtext: Yes, and they were also very carefully analysed in this house.

If that is so, I was not paying very much attention at the time. I still object to the principle of legislating by order in council and giving any person the powers contained in section 2(c) of the order to which reference has been made. It is possible to have the third degree; under that authority it is possible to compel men to sign documents upon which they may be subsequently prosecuted, and that is contrary to the first principles of British justice.

I should have liked to thank the hon. member for York-Sunbury for his remarks this afternoon in connection with our transportation system, had it not become evident early in his speech that he was attempting to use the situation at Prince Edward Island to discredit the members of this house coming from that province. I fully endorse everything that has been said by the minister for that province, the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Ralston); and in that connection I should like to add that it would not look very nice or be very courteous to the minister if the private members from Prince Edward Island were to come from his
IMr. Mitchell.]
office, after discussing the car ferry matter, and immediately ask him questions about it in this house.
You are hiding your light under a bushei.

Well, before I am through I will light your candle. I only want to point out that between 1930 and 1935, when the hon. member for York-Sunbury was a member of this house, a supporter of the Bennett government and a part-time minister, the people of Prince Edward Island did not know that he existed. While he was a member of the Bennett government he never rose in his place in this house and complained that the people of Prince Edward Island were getting only six cents a bushel for their potatoes. He never asked Mr. Bennett to put a floor under the price of Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick potatoes. He never complained about the fact that pork sold in Prince Edward Island for only 1J cents a pound during that period. He never complained that hides were sold for twenty-five cents each, not twenty-five cents a pound. He never complained that eggs were being sold at very low prices; he never complained that butter, on which he rode into power, was being used in Prince Edward Island for axle grease. The people of Prince Edward Island know all these things, and he will not deceive those people in the least. He tried1 that before on the island, but all I had to do was to tell the people just what I have said to-night, and they were quite satisfied that everything was all right. The hon. gentleman made a speech there just before the last provincial election, and his own party said that was the reason why they lost the election. I have told the people there that the hon. member for York-Sunbury made a mistake when he did not take up another calling. I said I thought the hon. gentleman should have joined the circus when he was a young man, taking the part of the fellow who never opened his mouth without putting his foot in it. The people of Prince Edward Island will not be hoodwinked by any person in this house who attempts to use the serious situation that exists there in order to get across to the people something that may be of some help to the Tories of that province.

Some reference was made to Captain Read being superannuated after forty years of faithful service to the public. I like to give credit where credit is due, and I would remind the hon. member for York-Sunbury that Captain Read navigated the icebreaker Earl Grey which was sold to the Russian government during the last war, that he piloted that boat safely across the Atlantic ocean, which was infested with submarines,

Supply-External Affairs
brought it safely to its destination and returned home. Captain Read has been a very courteous official; and though he made one mistake just two years before reaching the age of retirement, I think we should be a little charitable. If the Canadian National railways saw fit to grant Captain Read a pension, from the fund to which he contributed for many years, I think we should forget about the whole matter instead of airing it again in public.
The two ministers who have spoken, the Minister of Transport and the Minister of National Defence, have, I believe, covered the other phases of the car ferry situation. We all feel that a new ferry would be acceptable, and we hope to see one constructed at the very earliest possible date. I am sure we can entrust this to the Department of Munitions and Supply or the Department of Transport, to be attended to when the time is most suitable.

This afternoon and this evening we have heard from hon. members and members of the cabinet hailing from the mari-t.imes something about the Prince Edward Island ferry. Perhaps I might add a word, because I visited Prince Edward Island in 1941 for the first time in my life. It was a great privilege and a great pleasure. There may be other places where hospitality abounds to the same extent, but there is no place in Canada where more hospitality could be shown to one coming from another province. Without engaging in the controversy with respect to the ferry service, I wish to say that on my visit, and from communications and personal contact since that time, I have learned something of the feeling of the people of Prince Edward Island with respect to this problem.
If I may project myself into the debate to-night as one coming from one of the central provinces of Canada, I would say a word arising from my personal experience in connection with transportation problems between Tormentine and Borden. Sometimes people from other parts of Canada are too prone to think of Prince Edward Island as a far-distant province. As a result they may not be sufficiently interested in the problems of that island. But when the people of that province call out through their government and through their responsible citizens; when they call out through the various avenues by means of which they can raise their voices in their plea for better transportation facilities between the island and the mainland, they are not calling out for something in addition to what they require or in addition to what they are entitled to, but rather they ask for simple justice in a cause in respect of which simple justice must be given.
One of the things which struck me most forcibly in going from the mainland to the island and returning was the fact that there seemed to be such a perilous and slender thread of communication between the island and other parts of Canada. I was there in the fall of the year, and one could not help entertaining that thought when he saw the many freight cars, the vast quantities of products and the great number of automobiles awaiting transportation.
May I join with those who have raised their voices in support of the solution of a problem which has been so ably presented. As one from central Canada may I state that we, too, appreciate their problem. We would like to help Prince Edward Island, and it is my hope that the discussion in the committee to-day will contribute something toward giving better transportation for that magnificent portion of the dominion, that province known so affectionately in other parts of Canada as "the island".

To provide for Canadian share of expenses of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission appointed under treaty between Canada and the United States for the protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries of the Fraser river system- further amount required, $2,000.

This item is to provide a sum for the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission, which was appointed under treaty between Canada and the United States for the
1S12
Supply-Fisheries

protection, preservation and extension of the sockeye salmon fisheries of the Fraser river, in British Columbia. I have no quarrel with this vote. I think it is a proper one, and that the commission is doing excellent work.
But there is a situation arising with regard to the Fraser river salmon run which should be explained without further delay by the government. It has to do with a suggestion we see in the press to the effect that one of our large fishing companies has applied for licences to instal fish traps on the west coast of Vancouver Island, in what is known as the Sooke area. There are already five fish traps in the Sooke area, and the fish caught are from the Fraser river run.
I am sure all hon. members from British Columbia will want to know whether the government now proposes to allow more fish traps to be put in that area. It would of course affect the conservation of the salmon, but also it would be flying directly in the face of recommendations made on two occasions by the committee of this house on marine and fisheries. I regret exceedingly that the new Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bertrand) is not in his seat to-night, but in his absence probably the Minister of Transport (Mr. Michaud) can tell us the actual position.
I would remind him and the committee that when the standing committee on marine and fisheries sat in 1937 they were given instructions that they should consider the question of the advisability of the government issuing trap fishing licences in British Columbia waters. They had not been sitting long until it was unanimously agreed that there should be no additional fishing licences; on March 1, 1937, a resolution was passed by that committee, moved by myself and seconded by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) in the following terms:
That this committee go on record as opposed to any additional trap fishing licences in British Columbia, reserving the question of the advisability of renewing licences in the Sooke area for further consideration by this committee at the present time.
In other words, in the midst of our proceedings we agreed there should be no additional licences for trap fishing. We then went on to consider the question as to whether licences for existing traps should be continued. If the Minister of Transport will refer to page 207 of the minutes of proceedings of that committee in 1937 he will find that the chairman summed up the situation in these words, when referring to the resolution I have just read:
That would eliminate all the other waters and
confine us to this one question of whether the traps at Sooke should be continued or withdrawn.

In the report of the committee made od April 5, 1937, the following recommendation was made:
That no more trap licences be granted in British Columbia waters except in the so-called Sooke area, and concerning which we are unable to come to a decision as to whether they should be continued or not, without the opportunity of securing further information.
The Department of Fisheries subsequently made further investigations into whether these five licences should be continued. I think I am correct when I say that the standing committee really doubted very much whether even the five licences should be allowed. There was no thought of any more licences being granted in that area; they were certainly to be limited to five. Two years later, in 1939, the question was again referred to the standing committee on marine and fisheries. In that year the whole question under consideration was the continuance or the maintenance of the five licences which had been issued in previous years. I quote from page 256 of the minutes of the proceedings of the committee in 1939, as follows:
Hon. Mr. Michaud: If a judge, after taking the evidence of those advancing arguments and possibly looking into what has transpired on the American side of the line for the last four or seven years, recommends that the maintenance of traps there would induce the Americans to revert to their former policy of licensing traps and that it would be against public interest and the interest of the fishermen of British Columbia, there is no doubt that we would have to abide by such a recommendation.
In due course the committee of 1939 made its report, and we find that they recommended that there be set up a judicial commission to inquire into the whole question. The proposed terms of reference to the commission are set out in one of the paragraphs of the report as follows:
To fully investigate and hear evidence under oath, and to determine and report, whether or not it is in the public interest that trap-nets for the capture of salmon should continue to bt authorized in the Sooke area-
And so on. The committee in both years agreed that there should be no additional traps. In due course an investigation was authorized, the Honourable Mr. Justice Sloan of the court of appeal of British Columbia being named commissioner. In his report we find words to the same effect. I think it is clear from that report that he was only considering whether the five trap licences should be granted each year and was not dealing at all with the question of issuing additional licences.
Now we find that another company-it is a sound company, under efficient management and l have no quarrel with them or

Supply-Fisheries
with their employees-is applying for licences or, according to an answer made in the house the other day, is negotiating with the government. I would point out to the Minister of Transport that if licences are granted to this company, it will be only a matter of time before someone else will be wanting to get a licence. It may result in the United States licensing trap nets on the other side of the boundary, which we all agree would be a serious thing for the Canadian fishermen. It might upset the whole Fraser river salmon plans. The fishermen on the coast are greatly disturbed over this. These men have done a grand job during the war. New' men have taken over the boats formerly owned by the Japanese, and no one can question that they have done good work.
