As was pointed1 out by the Minister of Fisheries at the time he could not deal directly with the matter until application had been made for licences. As a matter of fact I would be a little critical of the provincial government for leasing some 8,000 acres of foreshore lands to British Columbia packers, knowing they were for fish traps and that the company would then make application to the dominion government for fishing licences for traps. I wish to point out to the member for Vancouver South that some representations were made to the government by at least four members from British Columbia, and 1 trust he took the same steps that we did, because to wait until the matter comes up in the house might have been too late. I think we did the proper thing, and I urge him to follow the same course immediately a matter of this kind comes up. The hon. member said, when he made his statement, that the question of the fishing traps had a bearing on Ihe work of the international fisheries com-nission. It has really little bearing on our task. I made my protest against the issuing of licences for traps on account of what might happen if traps were put in there. It would, to my mind, have the effect of reducing the livelihood of the fishermen on the Fraser river.
I would point out to this house the dangers that are going to arise in the years after 1945. Beginning with that year it will be the duty of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission to regulate the sockeye salmon fisheries on the Fraser river. It is of interest to note, and this pertains to the same question, that up until 1935 the United States had been taking something like sixty-five per cent Fraser river fish; that is, of the catch of fish coming through the straits and heading to the waters of the Fraser. But when they took the traps out of United States waters the reverse was the case, so that from 1935 and on up until the present time Canadian fishermen have been taking from sixty to sixty-five per cent of the catch as against thirty-five per cent to the United States. But in 1945 by the treaty the matter of distribution of the sockeye will come into the hands of the international Paoific salmon fisheries commission, and the catch then has to be divided equally between the two countries. This means that in 1945 or 1946 the sixty-five per cent of the fish which we have been taking will be reduced to fifty per cent of the total sockeye coming to the Fraser river. Hence, not as a member of the sockeye commission, but particularly as a member of this house representing a fisheries district, I felt it incumbent upon myself to 
make strong protests to the government against allowing any traps to be put in there and operated, because any traps put in there intercept the fish as they come in and thereby affect the livelihood of the fishermen. After all, only a certain number of fish come in, and the more traps you have, the fewer fish there will be each year for the individual fisherman. I do not think any definite statement has been made by the minister on this point other than that the representations we made are being given very serious consideration.
I do not think it is right for the provincial government to grant the application for a lease of 8,000 acres of foreshore lands to British Columbia Packers, knowing the conditions which will arise if fish traps are put in there.

As one of the four members from British Columbia who protested against the issue of these leases I should like to endorse what the two previous speakers have said. I would have been very much gratified if the Minister of Fisheries had been in his place to-night and had been able to give us the assurance asked for by the hon. member for Vancouver South. The Minister of Trans-nort, speaking apparently on behalf of the Minister of Fisheries, used an expression that gave me some feeling of doubt. He said that there had been no formal application for this licence. The use of the word "formal" might in days to come save him from any accusation of bad faith, because he might say that there was nothing formal, that there had been merely what are called in diplomatic circles conversations. But when a man in a high position promises something by way of conversation we generally expect to take his word as an undertaking.
But what makes it a little doubtful is this. Here is a big, powerful, shrewd company. They know all about the obstacles that have been placed in the way as mentioned by the hon. member for Vancouver South. They know it was practically agreed upon by resolution of the fisheries committee that there should be no more traps granted beyond those already in existence. And yet this shrewd company goes to the considerable expense of staking out some 8,130 acres of foreshore land to be leased from the provincial government. The procedure is that they must first obtain from the provincial government leases of the foreshore, which is the land between high and low water. Then they come to this government and ask for a licence to put in traps at these particular sites. It is remarkable that this company should go to such considerable expense because this land has to be surveyed, and so on, and advertised at considerable

Supply-Fisheries
expense in the Gazette and in the local papers. The seven applications cover nearly half a column of the Gazette.. If they do all that without having some assurance from some friend at court that they are likely to get a licence from the dominion government, they are certainly not proceeding along very businesslike lines. I have had some fear, as apparently the hon. member for New Westminster has had; but certainly we had some considerable hope that the matter might be adjusted favourably by refusing the licences entirely.
The argument put forward in the press by this company, which has taken considerable space in the papers to advocate its views, is that these traps would catch fish more readily than they could be caught by the fishermen and therefore they would produce more fish. They consider that an argument which might appeal just now if fishermen are scarce. As regards fishemen being scarce, I have a record here of the licences issued in the last two years. In 1941, when the Japs had a large number of licences, the total number of fishing licences in British Columbia-I am not talking of salmon licences alone-was 13,602, of which the Japs had 2,090. Of course the figures would be different if I confined them entirely to salmon. I have not those figures, but they would count still more strongly for the argument I intend1 to make. In 1942, all these Jap licences, numbering 2,090, were eliminated because the Japs were all removed from the coast and were not given any licence to fish. In 1942, in times of an almost unbelievable scarcity of labour of all kinds, much worse in British Columbia than in the east, the total number of licences issued was 15,380, all for whites or Indians-no Japs. So that not only was the loss of 2,090 Japs whose fishing licences were taken away absorbed, but there was an increase in the total number issued of some 1,700 odd, and that at a time of extreme scarcity of labour. That disposes of the idea that there is any need to increase the number of traps to catch more fish on the ground of a scarcity of fishermen.
Then as to the value of the fish caught last year, I have not the figures in tons or pounds, but the value taken last year greatly exceeded the value of the fish caught in the previous year. That was not altogether because more fish were taken, but on account of higher prices. To take it on the basis of the number of fish caught would not be a very fair test anyhow, because the run of salmon varies so much from year to year. But it is obvious that a great deal more in value of the fish caught was
obtained last year, with something like 1,700 more fishermen employed even after covering the loss of some 2,000 Japs. So that it does not appear that there is any justification whatever for this company asking for traps on the ground that they need them to catch the fish necessary' in Canada or for the British market at this time.
There is another argument. When this agitation started-it was largely begun by myself in 1936-there were sometimes three, sometimes four and sometimes five traps at Sooke. The fish went past those traps and then into Puget Sound1, in almost entirely United States waters. There were a large number of United States traps there, with the result that they took somewhere about sixty-five per cent of the total catch that went into the Fraser. For reasons which we need not go into, the United States government stopped the issue of all trap licences in Puget Sound1. The consequence was that we caught more fish than were caught on the American side- a desirable thing. The people who held the vested interest in those traps were very unwilling to part with them, and they saw', when an agitation was brought forward for more traps on our side, a chance to employ' this argument with their government, "Canada is catching the great bulk of them now; let us get our traps back." I had a letter from a man who owns traps on the United States side in which he says that he hopes our traps would be maintained and increased, because that would- be all the justification, they would need to go back to traps on the United States side. If we go on with the traps now proposed, it would be an invitation and almost a guarantee that the Americans would be allowed to put their traps back on their side, which would- reduce our catch materially. The obvious result would be to wipe out not all, but by far the greater number of our fishermen on the west coast. Salmon fishing, cf course, is the largest industry there; and when we think of the services these men have rendered in this war, how they have cheerfully given up their boats for naval- purposes, and have joined the -naval reserve, where they have done excellent service, it does not seem a very appropriate return for their gallantry, and the danger they are running, that while they are serving our country we take steps which would deprive them of their livelihood when they come back. If you want to go in for that kind- of thing, of course, the answer is, go ahead, forgetting justice and decency.
Remember this also, that if any more are allowed at Sooke, there is a sort of gentlemen's agreement, to which I was no party,

Supply-Fisheries
that the two or three traps there should be allowed to remain, but at any rate they were to be the only ones. If we add more there now, the logical reply is, "You must allow them all over British Columbia," and then you wipe out the working fishermen or reduce them to a very large extent. That is not a desirable thing.
When war came it was a very advantageous condition for us when we found this class of fishermen there, men who knew every corner and bay on the coast and possessed other valuable information. I do not want to give away war secrets, but it is well known that there have been submarines up the west coast in the vicinity of most of the fishing towns. A lighthouse was shelled a year ago, and also one or two vessels have been torpedoed. The services these fishermen have given have been very useful indeed. We must not let them down.
I wonder if I might take a moment to deal with another matter, one of burning importance. I am sorry the Minister of Fisheries is unavoidably absent just now. The subject is also connected with the Minister of National Revenue. Some years ago a sales tax was put upon gasoline sold to everybody on the Pacific coast, and more recently some special kind of revenue tax of three cents a gallon was imposed. The law-and I am not talking about custom or favouritism or anything of the kind, but the law which you and I can demand and invoke for our rights-says that if anyone clears from a customs port to go deep-sea fishing he does not have to pay these taxes. If they are engaged1 in deep-sea fishing they are exempt from the three cents and from the sales tax, which together represent a difference of 4-8 cents a gallon-call it five cents when you are about it. That, of course, is an advantage: it helps the fishermen and aids in the production of fish in these times, when they are so badly needed.
About four years ago, when this tax was first put on, I interested myself in the subject and found that this was the law; that anyone clearing for deep-sea could, by producing his deep-sea clearance, get his gas and oil at that reduced rate; but the trouble was that in order to clear you had to have a customs officer, and you do not have customs officers all over the coast, at rugged and isolated places, as fishing places so ofteu are. So that it was found desirable to appoint what I call amateur, though perhaps a better word would be acting, customs officers. Instead of having a customs officer at a salary of 81,200 a year, the habit grew up of paying someone a very small sum on

each boat he cleared. The total was not to exceed $200 a year, and never did, and after the fishing season was over, of course the man did not get any salary. I persuaded the. dominion government customs department to appoint these acting customs officers at a number of places. One was Bull Harbour and another was Winter Harbour. Probably one hundred and fifty boats got their gas and oil there during the season. A person of very ordinary ability could do this work; it was not necessary to have an expert. In two cases I had women appointed, because they happened to be at the right place and were quite capable of doing the work, which was slight. But they were required to clear every morning or night, as the case might be; when the fishermen came in at night they cleared for the next day, and they got their gas and oil much cheaper, and could engage in fair and1 helpful competition with the Americans. The arrangement worked very well indeed. Occasionally petty jealousies arose. Two oil stations quarreled as to in whose vicinity the acting customs officer should be placed, because naturally a fisherman would take his fish to the place which was nearest to where he cleared his boat, and it was an advantage to have one of these acting officials near an oil station or a fish buying plant, as the case might be. People are selfish. I recall one particular place where they complained to the government that I was not treating them fairly because I had put the customs officer a quarter of a mile nearer one plant than the other. I settled that matter by saying that, if there was any more of it, the likelihood was that the officer would be taken away altogether, and I would let the fishermen know who was responsible for its being closed. That led them to see common sense. Finally, I planted a customs officer at almost exactly half way between the two competing plants; and even then one of them wrote and complained that he was fifty yards nearer the other plant than he was to the writer's plant.
This sort of petty jealousy will arise anywhere. If you get a post office planted in a remote place there is always controversy as to just where it is to be located. What is the remedy? It is, I think, to handle it the way I did, and make some arrangement which will be mutually satisfactory. But the way it will be handled now will be totally different, and it is as to this injustice I wish to speak. In the district beyond mine there are two rival fish plants. Each wanted the officer at their place and not near the other man, and they made so much fuss to the department

Suppl y-Fish e lies
of customs that, to solve an annoying situation, the department said, "Oh, we will do away with the whole thing and confine it only to those very few stations where there is a permanent paid customs officer." Certainly that looked to be a ready and simple way of getting rid of an embarrassing situation, but it was a very poor way from the point of view of the fishermen or of justice. It would be an analogous situation if, because there was some trouble between myself and my neighbour as to where we would post our letters, an order was issued that there should be no post office there at all and that we would have to go twenty or thirty miles to post our mail. They have issued an order that almost all these stations except the permanent customs stations shall be wiped out. I can think of one case, Bull Harbour, where we had a woman acting for a few cents she received in connection with each application, and where the amount for the whole year would not exceed 8150.
One hundred and fifty fishermen got their oil and gas there for several months during the fishing season, and it was an enormous advantage.
These fishermen have to go out twenty or thirty or forty miles offshore before they begin fishing; that takes gas. They have to have good-sized boats capable of going out into the open Pacific. When they are fishing they have to keep the engine running all the time, because they fish by trolling lines. The boat must be kept moving slowly, and that takes more gas proportionately than proceeding at a higher speed. The gas forms a considerable part of their expense, and the price has gone up a good deal iu the last few years and even in the last few months. Now the Department of National Revenue comes along and merely to save a little trouble when people squabble about it they throw the whole thing over. That is not the way to do. They say,
' It would be no worse than farmers having to pay gasoline tax." I am not discussing the rival claims of farmers and fishermen, I am talking about the law. The law saj's I have the right to post my mail, and it says that these fishermen if they clear for the deep sea have this exemption. I do not propose to allow a thing of that kind to go through as long as I have a voice to protest; it is palpably unreasonable and unjust.
I understand it was dealt with by a committee. A committee consisting of whom? With one exception, of officials, members of the Department of National Revenue, who are not familiar with fishing conditions, do not have to be and do not want to be. They see these returns coming in and giving some trouble and bother, and they say, We will stop the whole thing. There was one member on the committee who understood fishing conditions, but he of course was overruled. I think if the matter were fully explained to the Minister of National Revenue, as I hope to have opportunity to do, a remedy will be found; and it is urgent, because the fishing is now going on.
As to Winter Harbour, we had a person there last year. Now what are they going to do? They have to go to Quatsino, some thirty-five miles away, where there is a permanent customs officer, and lose the time and gas that that involves. The life of a fisherman is like this: He starts about midnight in order to get to the fishing grounds at daybreak, because at that time and at dusk the fishing is best. He goes out there and fishes at dawn; he is twenty miles or more from home; he cannot go back, and therefore he hangs around out there in the heavy sea, perhaps catching an odd fish but hardly enough to pay for his gas. Then there is another hour or two along about sunset when the same favourable conditions arise. So that in the summer he has to stay there until about nine o'clock. Then he comes home the twenty or forty miles and waits in lino with thirty or forty or perhaps 100 other boats to sell his fish and have them weighed. Then he gets his groceries and gas permit and clears at the customs; then he goes and gets the gas, and then he can go to bed. He gets in, I suppose, about ten o'clock and has to leave about midnight. So that he has no time to go running around needlessly, .and, besides, if he did spend his time running to Quatsino, it vcould take him twelve hours to go there and back and there is a day's fishing gone, besides the cost of the gas. So that it is giving a premium to the two or three fishermen who happen to live in the immediate vicinity of these three or four permanent officers. I cannot see any justice or common sense or saving or war necessity in making this change, which, it seems to me, is due to lack of appreciation of the situation.
Therefore I plead with the government and the Minister of National Revenue-I have taken it up with the Minister of Fisheries, and I think I have his sympathy-and suggest that if they cannot do anything better at this late hour, at least let the situation continue as it is for another year. It has been that way now' for three or four years, and no harm has happened. For all the revenue they would get it would perhaps pay them to allow all the fishermen on the Pacific coast not to have to clear at alii. That would save the expense of maintaining these acting officers.
Be that as it may, at any rate I beg that they will take some steps to remedy the situation within the next few days, because the fishing is going on now, and the fishermen cannot go thirty miles to get their supplies. And we do want these people to catch fish. Britain

is crying out for it, and we have not enough fish to go round even in British Columbia; tinned fish is practically off the market. The whole of last year's output was sold to Britain. We want to help our practical fishermen in this way to maintain the output that they had in years gone by.

Those rates have remained the same to this time, with the exception that the $1 a day allowance to single men was increased to $1.25 when the allowance to the soldier living out of barracks was increased from $1 to $1.25. These rates had been fixed on a comparable basis with what was being paid to men going into the army. They have not been modified since. Representations had been made from time to time by men engaged on this work to the effect that they should receive the cost-of-living bonus; but, as lion, members know, there is no cost-of-living bonus for the soldier. The matter has been under discussion, but no decision favourable to the men has been reached yet in that regard.

In my opinion everything the minister has said in reply to my question indicates that there is a reason for very favour-
able consideration of the representations of these men. He has said there has been ho cost-of-living bonus given to the men in the army, but I think he forgets that within the last few months they have been given an increase in pay amounting to twenty cents a day. However, the situations are not comparable, because men in the army receive dental and medical care, and attentions of that kind. On the other hand, these special constables receive nothing more than their $3.20. and they have families to keep.

I do not wish to delay the committee, but I shall have something to say on this point when the main estimates are before the committee. However, I think the minister will agree with me when I say that when the history of this war is written, so far as the home front is concerned, a very bright page will be reserved for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in this war-time period. They have done a magnificent job. Perhaps it is unnecessary for members of parliament even to refer to their work, because it speaks for itself.
Between now and the presentation of the main estimates I would ask the minister to consider this question of cost-of-living bonus for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. It is not good enough to say that men in the armed forces are getting a certain amount, and that for that reason members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police should be placed on a comparable basis. If in our war effort we were to base our remuneration upon what is received by the armed forces we would have before us an interesting comparison. The opinion has been expressed in the house on many occasions-I have so expressed it-that there is a great disparity between the pay and allowances of our armed forces and the rates of pay of those engaged in the civilian war effort.
I would ask the minister to give conscien-lious consideration to this matter, if for no other reason than that of a gesture of goodwill from the hearts of the Canadian people who, in this lime of war, have felt a sense of security and safety on our home front. I believe any favourable consideration on the part of the minister would be greatly appreciated.

Is it not a fact that the increase in pay was really to take the place of the subsistence allowance paid to the member of the mounted police force, himself, and that it disregarded entirely any dependents he might have? Is it not a fact that in dealing with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police the government has not taken into consideration the dependents of the men? Are not the regulations such that a mounted policeman cannot take unto himsalf a wife without the consent of the authorities, or until he has served a certain time in the service and is receiving a sum adequate to support a wife and family?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: That has been the regulation since the organization of the force. The rule has been similar to that applied in banks. It is necessary for a man to attain a certain rank and receive a certain pay which will enable him to support a wife and a family according to the standard which should be that of a member of the force.

They do not take the dependents into consideration; only the man himself?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The increase in the total amount paid to the married man is different from that granted to the single man. It was not really an increase in pay, it was an increase in that part of what he receives in substitution of rations, lodging, light and fuel for himself and for his family, if he is a married man, and for himself alone, if he is single.

Is an additional allowance made for each child?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. These conversions have been on an arbitrary basis. There are men of the Royal Canadian Mounted
Police in barracks whose actual cost of living is several dollars a day. I was horrified the other day at having to approve the purchase of coal at $40 a ton. Members of the force are stationed at different places and provided with lodging, rations, light and fuel at considerable expense. Since they are subject to income tax this situation is recognized and for taxation purposes, no matter what the cost may be, only the value under normal conditions is considered as income and subject to taxation.

A moment ago the
minister indicated that the authorities would study the situation to see whether these men could get along on the amount that was allowed to them. By what standard does the department endeavour to judge whether a man can get along?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The devotion of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to duty has always been outstanding. It has always been recognized that they were receiving pay and allowances merely to carry them along. The pension provisions were made more generous than those of any other branch of the civil service, as some compensation in respect Of that fact.

In my judgment the
pay of the mounted police and the constables is altogether too low, and a revision upward is overdue.
Item agreed to.

The Secretary of State
(Mr. McLarty) is not here to-night, but perhaps the Minister of Trade and Commerce would indicate why a further amount is required.

The Secretary of State was called to Toronto, and he asked me to answer this question. The additional amount is required for salaries and bonuses for additional employees of the bureau for translations whose services are required by various war departments.
Item agreed to.

1/39. Purchase of the steamer Pelee to maintain the Pelee island and mainland service, $40,000.

Would the minister indicate when the steamer Pelee was purchased and what vessel it replaced?

Supply-S team ship Subventions

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade andi Commerce):
speechtext:
The steamer Pelee
was purchased in 1914 and was specially built for the service. The service was subsidized by the government for some years at $11,000 a year. This subsidy was then reduced to $4,000. About a year ago the man holding the contract laid up the vessel because he found he could not operate under the subsidy agreement. Efforts were made to secure another vessel, but without avail, and inasmuch as the service had to be maintained with Pelee island and1 no other vessel was available, it was decided to try to purchase this vessel. This was done, after valuations had been made, at a price of $40,000. We then made an arrangement to sell the vessel to the same man, Mr. Goodiison of Blenheim, Ontario. We have entered into an arrangement with him to continue this service. He has purchased the vessel, the purchase price being payable $10,000 on October 31, 1942, which has been paid, and the balance at the rate of $5,000 a year.

The minister said that
the steamer had been purchased in 1914; does he mean it was purchased by the private owner?

I
said it was specially built in 1914 for this service.

I thought the minister
said it was purchased.

Is the new subsidy on
the reduced basis of $4,000?
The subsidy has been increased for this service.
To what figure?
To

To the original figure.
This is an increase to the new purchaser who purchased the boat from the government about a year ago? This man purchased the boat for $40,000, payable $10,000 down and the rest in regular payments. The subsidy has been increased from $4,000 to $11,000.
That was the best arrangement we could make to maintain the service with Pelee island.
Was the same offer made to the previous owner of the vessel who had laid it up on account of inadequate subsidy?

The vessel was laid up because the owner found that he could not operate the service with the
[Mr. Graydon.l
subsidy being paid. The net result was that the government purchased the vessel and made an arrangement with him for repurchase at the same amount and granted an increased subsidy.
He pays out of the earnings he gets under the new contract? He paid $10,000, and then he pays the balance as he receives the money from the government.
I think the two arrangements are entirely separate. The sale of the boat to the operator for an amount equal to the price paid by the government was a separate arrangement.
These payments are not spread? The payments are made as the operator of the boat gets his subsidy from the government. One is tied in with the other?
We pay the subsidy, and we see that he makes his payments. If he got behind in his payments we would withhold the subsidy.

I should like to get this clear. It seems to be becoming more confused as we go along. First of all, the vendor of the boat received $40,000 from the government for his boat. The government paid him $40,000 in cash. Is that correct?
Yes.

Then the next stage in the transaction is that the man starts to buy .the boat back from the government. He has still the $40,000 in his right-hand pants' pocket. He also gets his subsidy raised from $4,000 to $11,000. Then he starts to buy the boat back from the government out of this increased subsidy from $4,000 to $11,000 which he is paid every year. As I say, he still has the $40,000 in the bank. Then he proceeds to carry out his contract on a time-payment plan. Does the minister regard that as good business?

Yes, I do. The Pelee was offered for sale after being laid up because the owner could not operate the service at the subsidy then being paid by the government. The Pelee was offered for sale at a cash price of $40,000, and under instructions of the department her value was appraised by Lloyds surveyor in Toronto, who found after a complete survey that the vessel was in good condition and reported that a valuation of $40,000 was fair and reasonable. Under present war conditions it appeared

Supply-Steamship Subventions
impossible to find anyone who would buy this vessel for cash and place her on the Pelee route under subsidy. Since it was urgently necessary that a vessel of this type be procured without further delay, the minister recommended that the department be authorized to purchase the Pelee at a cost of $40,000. This was done under authority of order in council P.C. 8795, of September 30, 1942. The vessel was then resold to Mr. D. L. Goodison, who entered into a contract with the department to operate the Pelee island mainland service for a period of six years.
840,000 is the amount for which the government bought it?
Yes; everything is perfectly open.
I am not suggesting that it is not. But it seems a strange contract.

He is to operate the service for a period of six years at $11,000 a year under the following terms: The price is $40,000, and the government takes security for that with a mortgage on the vessel. The government concluded this arrangement with the purchaser, giving him an increased subsidy, in order to maintain the service which was considered necessary. We had to make the best possible arrangement we could.

It is getting late, and I do not want to delay the passage of the item, but it is very unfortunate that it comes up at this time of the evening. I would ask the minister this question: Did he or his department consider the possibility of increasing the subsidy from $4,000 to $11,000, and allowing the owner still to retain ownership of the vessel? That would have involved no undertaking from the government other than the increase in the subsidy which the government has obligated itself to pay. I know nothing about this particular transaction. It may be perfectly in order in every way, but on its face it does not look very good. It brings up this point. We as a government, in my opinion, and I will express it perhaps more volubly at some other stage of the session, have paid out far too much money in capital investments in Canada during this wartime period. We have invested tremendous sums of money in buildings all over Canada when we might have rented buildings in many places, and when we might have made other arrangements in many other instances. The practice is far too prevalent of making these capital investments. I ask the minister again: Did he consider leaving the ownership of this boat
with the owner and simply increasing the subsidy with no further obligation from the government?
I have no doubt that the question raised by the leader of the opposition was very carefully and thoroughly considered by the capable people in the department.
Did the minister himself go into that transaction?
Yes; I was in constant consultation with my officials, and we made the very best possible arrangement we could to carry on this service.
The minister is a good business man. Did any question arise in his mind as to the propriety of this transaction from a business point of view?
Not the slightest.

Surely the minister will agree that to buy a man's boat for $40,000 cash and) then sell the boat back to him on a time-payment plan and give him an increased subsidy from $4,000 to $11,000 is at least suspicious-looking.
Only to a suspicious mind, I think.
I am afraid my business experience does not agree with that of the minister.

I do not think the minister has made any too good a deal. Here is a man who cannot make his boat go on a $4,000 a year subsidy. He then sells it to the government for $40,000 cash. The government then turns round and sells the boat back to him for $40,000 to be repaid over a number of years, and increases his subsidy from $4,000 to $11,000 for a period of six years. So that the man gets $66,000 in subsidy, pays back $40,000 in six years, and that leaves him a working capital of $26,000 which is exactly what he had before. The net result is that he is operating the boat now for exactly the same subsidy as he had before, but when he gets through with his contract he will be $40,000 ahead because he will own the boat. If he could not run the service before on that subsidy, how in the world can he do so now? It means that he has done the government out of the price of that boat in the six years, and that does not look like good business to me. The minister may have been acting in perfectly good faith in the transaction, but I think he had one slipped over on him.



Supply-Steamship Subventions
Not at all. The government at the end of this transaction will not be out one dollar.
The government will be out the boat.

No; we did not have a boat to start with, and we are not finishing up with a boat. There is only one point to the whole transaction, namely, that in order to get the service, it was necessary to increase the subsidy and to make this arrangement with the contractor.
What was the former subsidy?

The contractor was paid $11,000 for some years. Then the government in its wisdom decided that the subsidy should be reduced, but the owner found1 that he could not operate his boat on the reduced subsidy and laid his boat up.
The subsidy was reduced to what?
Then the government had to increase it.
We found it necessary to revert to the original subsidy we were paying.

The minister says that they gave the contractor a subsidy of $11,000 at first, and then they decided in their wisdom to reduce it to $4,000. Am I right in that? Surely the government would never, without a thorough investigation, have decreased the subsidy from $11,000 to $4,000. That is a tremendous decrease. They must have had some good ground other than that, because a fellow says, "I will not operate that service", the government turns round and makes this transaction, restoring the subsidy to the original $11,000.
After negotiations.

It means that he is forcing the government to pay for that boat over again. The government have sold back the boat, but they have increased the subsidy by $7,000. It pays for the boat, and he is getting the amount he had before. He is operating exactly the same as he did before; only he is getting the payments of the boat clear.
No. The boat is being purchased by us for $40,000 and resold for $40,000. If these payments are kept up, and I have no doubt they will be, that settles that transaction.
But he has $40,000 in his pocket.

Will the hon. member pardon me? We have contracted with this owner to carry on this service for a subsidy of $11,000 a year, it having been found impossible to maintain the service at the reduced subsidy. That is the complete story; that is what was finally accomplished. But the negotiations in connection with this service cover a very considerable length of time, and the best possible arrangement we could make to give the people of this island connection with the mainland-and this was the only connection-was according to the terms of this agreement.

Surely, if it was found out that this man could not operate on the $4,000 subsidy, it would have been much more businesslike, instead of giving the increased subsidy of $11,000, to have investigated, and if you found that he could not make it go for $4,000, to have said to him, " We will give you $5,000," and let him operate on that.
He would not take it.

But instead of that, you increase the subsidy by about $7,000. When he sold you the boat he got $40,000 and stuck it in his pocket. Now he comes back and says, " I will not operate unless you give me $11,000," and $7,000 of the $11,000 is used to pay on the boat. The government is paying that, and the other $4,000 is left as operating expenses.
No.

That is certainly so, and at the end of the period the government is paying for that boat again and the man has $40,000 in his pocket and $4,000 on which to operate the boat. If that is not a nice piece of business for him, I should like to know what is.

m. Maritime Freight Rates Act-To hereby authorize and provide for the payment from time to time during the fiscal year 1942-43 to the Canadian National Railway Company of the difference (estimated by the Canadian National Railway Company and certified by the auditors of the said company to the Minister of Transport, as and when required by the said minister) occurring on account of the application of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, between the tariff tolls and the normal tolls (upon the same basis as set out in section 9 of the said act with respect to companies therein referred to) on all traffic moved during the calendar year 1942 under the tariffs approved on the eastern lines (as referred to in section 2 of the said act) of the Canadian National Railways-further amount required, $684,861.04.

What was the amount originally provided under the Maritime Freight Rates Act? I notice there is quite an important further amount required here, and I was wondering what the original amount was, and why it was increased?

Under the terms of the act, twenty per cent of the freight rates have to be reimbursed to the Canadian National Railways and other railways, and the net amount required each year is difficult to estimate at the beginning of the year. It has been the practice every year to vote some $3,350,000, and it was voted last year as in the past. During the year it developed that the traffic and the volume of freight in the maritimes were much larger than in the past, and therefore a larger contribution on the basis of twenty per cent had to be made. This is the net difference between the amount voted last year and the amount which is due the Canadian National Railways.
Largely on account of war-time conditions, I suppose?
Yes.
